o: A second judicial punishment for the same offence
Prosecution and punishment by a court
11.x: Article 20(2) covers prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal, but it does not extend to departmental proceedings.
11.tq: Identify the exception by distinguishing judicial punishment from departmental action.
11.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

11.s:
With reference to Article 20(3), consider the following statements:
1. It applies to criminal proceedings.
2. It covers oral and documentary testimony.
3. It generally treats fingerprints and physical specimens as testimonial self-incrimination.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
11.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Physical evidence such as fingerprints is not treated as testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3), as recognised in Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961).
11.tq: Separate testimonial evidence from physical evidence before selecting the combination.
11.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

11.s: Which of the following forms of evidence was held not to be covered by the protection against self-incrimination in Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961)?
o: A compelled written statement describing the offence
11.x: Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961) distinguished physical evidence such as fingerprints from testimonial compulsion protected by Article 20(3).
11.tq: Confusable-pair discrimination between physical evidence and testimony.
11.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

11.s: In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that which of the following, when conducted without consent, violates Article 20(3)?
o: Verification of age through official records
11.x: Selvi (2010) held that narco-analysis, polygraph examination and brain-mapping without consent violate the protection against testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3).
11.tq: Direct case-to-doctrine recall using physical-evidence distractors.
11.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

11.s: Which of the following correctly describes the applicability of Article 20?
o: It is available only during an Emergency.
It is available only to Indian citizens.
It is available to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies.
It is available only to natural persons present in India.
11.x: The protections under Article 20 are available to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies, subject to the nature of the particular protection.
11.tq: Membership and coverage trap involving citizens, aliens and companies.
11.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

11.s: Which one of the following is NOT covered by Article 20 protections?
o: Double prosecution and punishment for the same offence
11.x: Article 20 does not cover retrospective civil or tax laws. Article 20(1) is confined to ex post facto criminal laws.
11.tq: Find the excluded category by separating criminal law from civil and tax law.
11.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

11.s: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, the provision corresponding to the protection against double jeopardy is contained in:
11.x: Section 337 of the BNSS contains the provision relating to double jeopardy; it corresponds to the earlier Section 300 of the CrPC.
11.tq: Section-number discrimination between the new code and the repealed CrPC provision.
11.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

11.s: The protections under Article 20 are regarded as non-suspendable during an Emergency. Which of the following best reflects this position?
o: Article 20 protections may be suspended by executive order alone.
Article 20 applies only after the Emergency is withdrawn.
Article 20 protects only citizens during an Emergency.
Article 20 protections continue even during an Emergency.
11.x: The protections guaranteed by Article 20 are non-suspendable during an Emergency. They are not confined to citizens alone.
11.tq: Apply the constitutional protection to an Emergency situation without confusing it with ordinary restrictions.
11.sec: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain  [APPSC]

11.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Common Cause
B. P. Rathinam
C. Gian Kaur
D. Aruna Shanbaug
11.x: P. Rathinam was decided in 1994, Gian Kaur in 1996, Aruna Shanbaug in 2011 and Common Cause in 2018.
11.tq: Use the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two intervening rulings.
11.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

11.s: What was the ruling in P. Rathinam (1994)?
o: A fundamental right to marry was recognised.
Passive euthanasia was permitted under High Court supervision.
Section 309 IPC was upheld without qualification.
Section 309 IPC, dealing with attempted suicide, was held unconstitutional.
11.x: P. Rathinam (1994) held Section 309 IPC unconstitutional and treated suicide as something that should not be criminally punished.
11.tq: Direct case-holding recall with nearby euthanasia rulings as distractors.
11.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

11.s: Which case overruled the decision in P. Rathinam and held that there is no right to die, while recognising a right to die with dignity?
11.x: Gian Kaur v. State of Punjab (1996) overruled P. Rathinam. It held that there is no right to death but recognised the right to die with dignity and upheld Section 309 IPC.
11.tq: Identify the overruling case by separating right to die from right to die with dignity.
11.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

11.s:
Consider the following statements about the right to die and euthanasia cases:
1. Maruti Shripati Dubal held that the right to die formed part of Article 21.
2. Gian Kaur overruled the position in Maruti Shripati Dubal and P. Rathinam.
3. Common Cause recognised the right to die with dignity as a fundamental right under Article 21.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
11.x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Gian Kaur overruled P. Rathinam, but the material does not state that it overruled Maruti Shripati Dubal in the same formulation; the Bombay High Court decision preceded Rathinam.
11.tq: Avoid overextending an overruling judgment beyond the specific case identified.
11.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

11.s: Which of the following correctly describes the decision in Aruna Shanbaug (2011)?
o: The euthanasia plea was rejected, but passive euthanasia was allowed under strict conditions and High Court supervision.
A living will was declared invalid in every circumstance.
Active euthanasia was made a general fundamental right.
11.x: In Aruna Shanbaug (2011), the plea was rejected, but passive euthanasia was permitted under strict conditions and High Court supervision.
11.tq: Distinguish passive euthanasia from active euthanasia and from the later living-will ruling.
11.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

11.s: The validity of a living will or advance directive in the context of the right to die with dignity was recognised in:
11.x: Common Cause (2018) recognised the right to die with dignity as part of Article 21 and upheld the validity of a living will or advance directive.
11.tq: Direct identification of the latest landmark holding in a sequence of related cases.
11.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

11.s: With regard to attempted suicide in India, which of the following statements is correct?
o: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 created a general offence of attempted suicide.
The BNS decriminalised every act intended to compel a public servant.
The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 decriminalised attempted suicide in effect, and the BNS has no general offence of attempted suicide.
The BNS retained Section 309 IPC unchanged as a general offence.
11.x: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 decriminalised attempted suicide in effect. The BNS, in force from 1 July 2024, contains no general offence of attempted suicide.
11.tq: Compare the position under the Mental Healthcare Act and the post-IPC BNS framework.
11.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

11.s: Under Section 226 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, an attempt to commit suicide is punishable when it is made for the purpose of:
o: Compelling or restraining a public servant from discharging official duties
11.x: Section 226 BNS applies only to an attempt to compel or restrain a public servant from exercising lawful powers or discharging official duties; it is not a general offence of attempted suicide.
11.tq: Apply the narrow statutory exception instead of treating it as a general prohibition.
11.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

11.s: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaced the Indian Penal Code with effect from:
11.x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on 1 July 2024. It does not retain a general offence of attempted suicide corresponding to Section 309 IPC.
11.tq: Date-based recall of the transition from IPC to BNS.
11.sec: Right to die and euthanasia cases  [APPSC]

11.s: Which one of the following best distinguishes ‘procedure established by law’ from ‘due process of law’ in the context of Article 21?
o: The former examines the fairness of law, whereas the latter examines only legislative enactment
The former requires a procedure enacted by the legislature, whereas the latter also examines whether the procedure is fair and reasonable
The former applies only to preventive detention, whereas the latter applies only to civil rights
Both expressions have exactly the same meaning in Indian constitutional law
11.x: ‘Procedure established by law’ requires compliance with a law enacted by the legislature. ‘Due process of law’ additionally requires the law and procedure to satisfy standards of fairness and reasonableness.
11.tq: Discriminate between two closely related constitutional expressions by identifying the additional fairness test.
11.sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

11.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the A.K. Gopalan case:
1. It was decided in 1950.
2. It held that Article 21 protected an individual only against executive action.
3. It accepted that courts could examine the reasonableness of every law affecting personal liberty.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
11.x: The A.K. Gopalan decision was delivered in 1950 and treated Article 21 as protection mainly against executive action. It did not permit courts to examine the reasonableness of the law in the later Maneka Gandhi sense.
11.tq: Find the statement that reverses the limited approach adopted in the earlier case.
11.sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

11.s: Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional position after Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)?
o: Article 21 was confined exclusively to executive action
The Court rejected all elements of due process from Article 21
The procedure affecting life or personal liberty must be fair, just and reasonable
Articles 14, 19 and 21 were treated as completely independent of one another
11.x: The Maneka Gandhi decision held that a procedure affecting life or personal liberty must be fair, just and reasonable and must not be arbitrary.
11.tq: Identify the precise judicial test introduced by the later landmark judgment.
11.sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

11.s: The expression ‘golden triangle’ of fundamental rights refers to the interrelationship among which Articles?
11.x: Maneka Gandhi established a close relationship among Articles 14, 19 and 21, commonly described as the golden triangle of fundamental rights.
11.tq: Recall the standard constitutional grouping associated with the Maneka Gandhi doctrine.
11.sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

11.s: Which one of the following is a major difference between the A.K. Gopalan and Maneka Gandhi approaches to Article 21?
o: A.K. Gopalan introduced American due process, whereas Maneka Gandhi restored the Japanese approach
A.K. Gopalan excluded legislative action from scrutiny under Article 21, whereas Maneka Gandhi extended protection against arbitrary legislation
A.K. Gopalan linked Articles 14, 19 and 21, whereas Maneka Gandhi separated them
A.K. Gopalan dealt with preventive detention, whereas Maneka Gandhi dealt only with property rights
11.x: A.K. Gopalan treated Article 21 narrowly and did not subject legislation to the later fairness review. Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 also protects against arbitrary legislative action.
11.tq: Compare the two cases across the exact dimensions of legislative scrutiny and Article 21 protection.
11.sec: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

11.s:
Under Article 22(1) and Article 22(2), a person subjected to an ordinary arrest has which of the following rights?
1. To be informed of the grounds of arrest
2. To consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice
3. To be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, excluding journey time
Which of the statements given above are correct?
11.x: Article 22(1) and 22(2) provide all three safeguards in the case of an ordinary arrest: information about the grounds, legal representation, and production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours excluding journey time.
11.tq: Check the complete constitutional package of safeguards rather than selecting only one arrest right.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s: The safeguards under Article 22(1) and Article 22(2) are not available to which of the following persons under Article 22(3)?
o: A person produced before a magistrate within 24 hours
An enemy alien and a person detained under a preventive detention law
A person arrested under an ordinary warrant
Every person arrested for a criminal offence
11.x: Article 22(3) excludes an enemy alien and a person detained under a preventive detention law from the safeguards in Article 22(1) and 22(2).
11.tq: Use the constitutional exceptions to ordinary-arrest safeguards as the decisive pair.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s: Which of the following is NOT covered by the ordinary-arrest safeguards under Article 22(1) and Article 22(2)?
11.x: The listed situations—arrest under court orders, civil arrest and deportation of aliens—are not covered by the ordinary-arrest safeguards under Article 22(1) and 22(2).
11.tq: Test the scope of an exception by identifying all situations excluded from the ordinary-arrest guarantee.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which provisions correspond broadly to the earlier CrPC provisions concerning communication of grounds of arrest and production before a magistrate?
o: Sections 47 and 58; earlier Sections 50 and 57 of the CrPC
Sections 50 and 57; earlier Sections 47 and 58 of the CrPC
Sections 22 and 24; earlier Sections 20 and 21 of the CrPC
Sections 58 and 60; earlier Sections 47 and 50 of the CrPC
11.x: Sections 47 and 58 of the BNSS correspond broadly to the earlier CrPC Sections 50 and 57 concerning the relevant arrest safeguards.
11.tq: Discriminate between present BNSS section numbers and their earlier CrPC counterparts.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s: Which one of the following best describes preventive detention?
o: Detention based on suspicion of future acts and imposed without a criminal trial
Detention exclusively for non-payment of a civil debt
Detention after conviction for the purpose of executing a sentence
Detention ordered only by a criminal court after a finding of guilt
11.x: Preventive detention is detention without trial based on the apprehension that a person may commit specified harmful acts in the future. Punitive detention follows conviction.
11.tq: Separate preventive detention from punitive detention by focusing on timing and purpose.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s: A person detained under a preventive detention law may ordinarily be detained beyond three months only when:
o: An Advisory Board reports sufficient cause for continued detention
The President personally reviews the detention
The detainee waives the right of representation
The police commissioner grants written permission
11.x: Article 22(4) requires an Advisory Board, consisting of High Court judges or persons qualified to be High Court judges, to report sufficient cause before preventive detention continues beyond three months.
11.tq: Ask which constitutional authority supplies the mandatory safeguard for extended preventive detention.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s:
Consider the following statements regarding preventive detention under Article 22:
1. The grounds of detention must be communicated to the detainee.
2. The detainee must be given the earliest opportunity to make a representation against the order.
3. Parliament may prescribe the maximum period for which a person may be detained under a preventive detention law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
11.x: Article 22(5) requires communication of grounds and the earliest opportunity for representation. Article 22(7) permits Parliament to prescribe the maximum period of preventive detention in the circumstances specified by the Constitution.
11.tq: Combine safeguards under Article 22(5) with Parliament’s power under Article 22(7).
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 reduced the constitutional period for preventive detention without an Advisory Board report from three months to:
11.x: The 44th Amendment reduced the period from three months to two months. However, the relevant provision has not been notified, so the three-month period continues to operate.
11.tq: Distinguish the amended constitutional text from the provision that is actually in force.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s: Why does the three-month period continue to apply to preventive detention despite the 44th Amendment?
o: The Supreme Court struck down the two-month provision
Article 22 does not contain any period relating to an Advisory Board
The amended provision was never notified
11.x: Although the 44th Amendment substituted two months for three months, the relevant amended clause has never been notified. Consequently, the three-month rule continues to apply.
11.tq: Use the implementation-status trap: distinguish an enacted amendment from a notified and operative provision.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s: Which subject–legislative competence pair is correctly matched in relation to preventive detention?
o: Defence, foreign affairs and security of India — Parliament alone; public order and security of a State — Parliament and the States
Defence and foreign affairs — States alone; public order — Parliament alone
Public order — Parliament alone; security of India — States alone
Supplies essential to the community — States alone in every circumstance
11.x: Parliament alone legislates on preventive detention connected with defence, foreign affairs and the security of India. Parliament and the States may legislate on public order, security of a State and supplies essential to the community.
11.tq: Start from the sure exclusive Union subjects and then match the concurrent preventive-detention subjects.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s: Preventive detention is constitutionally justified under Article 22 in relation to which of the following?
o: Mere law and order in every local dispute
Any administrative inconvenience caused by an individual
Public order, but not merely routine law and order
Only a civil disagreement between private parties
11.x: The Supreme Court has distinguished public order from ordinary law and order. Preventive detention cannot be justified merely by routine law-and-order concerns.
11.tq: Use the higher-threshold comparison between public order and ordinary law and order.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s:
Arrange the following preventive detention laws in chronological order of enactment:
A. National Security Act
B. Maintenance of Internal Security Act
C. Preventive Detention Act
D. Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act
11.x: The Preventive Detention Act was enacted in 1950, MISA in 1971, COFEPOSA in 1974 and the National Security Act in 1980.
11.tq: Place the laws by their enactment years, using the earliest and latest items first.
11.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

11.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: NSA, 1980 — State law applicable only in Kerala
Preventive Detention Act, 1950 — First preventive detention law; lapsed in 1969
11.x: The Preventive Detention Act, 1950 was the first such law and lapsed in 1969. MISA was repealed in 1978, COFEPOSA concerns smugglers and foreign-exchange offenders, and NSA is a central law.
11.tq: Find the correctly matched law by checking both its date and its distinctive legal purpose or status.
11.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

11.s: The Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), 1971 is associated with which of the following?
o: Detention of foreign-exchange offenders and repeal in 1969
Its use during the Emergency and repeal in 1978
A state preventive detention law operating only in Jammu and Kashmir
A law enacted in 1980 for detention up to twelve months
11.x: MISA was enacted in 1971, used during the Emergency and repealed in 1978.
11.tq: Link the statute with its distinctive historical context and repeal year.
11.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

11.s: Which preventive detention law is specifically associated with suspected smugglers and foreign-exchange manipulators?
11.x: The Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974, or COFEPOSA, targets suspected smugglers and foreign-exchange offenders.
11.tq: Use the subject-matter clue in the statute’s title to identify the correct law.
11.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

11.s: Which of the following statements about the National Security Act, 1980 is correct?
o: It permits detention up to twelve months without charges
It is a state law applicable only to Kerala
It was repealed in 1978 after the Emergency
It was the first preventive detention law and lapsed in 1969
11.x: The National Security Act, 1980 permits preventive detention for up to twelve months without charges, subject to constitutional and statutory safeguards.
11.tq: Match the statute with its distinctive maximum detention period rather than its general name.
11.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

11.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with UAPA?
o: UAPA, 1967 — Kerala’s state preventive detention law
UAPA, 1967 — Law exclusively concerning foreign exchange
UAPA, 1967 — First preventive detention law, lapsed in 1969
11.x: The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 is associated with terrorism and unlawful associations. The other descriptions relate to different laws.
11.tq: Avoid the law-name swap by matching UAPA with its stated anti-terror and unlawful-associations role.
11.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

11.s: Which of the following pairs consists entirely of State preventive detention laws?
11.x: The Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act and the Kerala Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act are state-level preventive detention laws. NSA, COFEPOSA, MISA, UAPA and the Preventive Detention Act are central enactments.
11.tq: Classify laws by territorial level and eliminate central statutes from the state-law pair.
11.sec: Preventive detention laws - names

11.s: The historical roots of preventive detention legislation in India are associated with which pair?
o: The Charter Act of 1813 and the Indian Councils Act of 1909
Regulation III of 1818 and the Rowlatt Act
The Government of India Act, 1935 and the States Reorganisation Act, 1956
The Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951
11.x: Regulation III of 1818 and the Rowlatt Act are identified as important historical roots of preventive detention legislation in India.
11.tq: Recall the historically paired antecedents instead of later constitutional or electoral enactments.
11.sec: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

11.s: Which constitutional change was introduced by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 in relation to Articles 20 and 21 during a National Emergency?
o: It made both Articles 20 and 21 unenforceable during every Emergency
It transferred the power under Article 359 from the President to the Supreme Court
It removed Article 21 from the list of Fundamental Rights
It ensured that an order under Article 359 could not suspend the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21
11.x: The 44th Amendment inserted the protection that the right to move courts for enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended by an order under Article 359, even during a National Emergency.
11.tq: Identify the amendment’s protective effect and reject the reversal that makes Articles 20 and 21 unenforceable.
11.sec: Articles 20 and 21 during emergency - suspension status and amending act

11.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable during a National Emergency.
2. The protection relating to Articles 20 and 21 was inserted into Article 359 by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
3. The President may suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of every Fundamental Right during an Emergency.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
11.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Article 359 does not permit suspension of the right to enforce Articles 20 and 21; its operation concerns other Fundamental Rights subject to constitutional limits.
11.tq: Spot the overbroad word ‘every’ in the statement about the President’s Article 359 power.
11.sec: Articles 20 and 21 during emergency - suspension status and amending act

11.s: The 44th Amendment’s protection of Articles 20 and 21 was principally a constitutional response to which development?
11.x: The 44th Amendment responded to the ADM Jabalpur decision of 1976, which had permitted suspension of the right to life and personal liberty during the Emergency.
11.tq: Link the corrective constitutional amendment with the earlier judicial decision it sought to address.
11.sec: Articles 20 and 21 during emergency - suspension status and amending act

11.s: Which judgment overruled the approach of ADM Jabalpur concerning the right to life and personal liberty?
o: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
11.x: The K.S. Puttaswamy judgment of 2017 overruled the approach taken in ADM Jabalpur concerning the suspension of Article 21 protections.
11.tq: Distinguish the later corrective privacy judgment from the earlier Article 21 cases.
11.sec: Articles 20 and 21 during emergency - suspension status and amending act

11.s: Which additional change relating to a National Emergency was made by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978?
o: The ground of ‘internal disturbance’ under Article 352 was replaced by ‘armed rebellion’
The ground of ‘armed rebellion’ under Article 352 was replaced by ‘internal disturbance’
The power to proclaim an Emergency was transferred exclusively to the Supreme Court
11.x: The 44th Amendment replaced ‘internal disturbance’ with the more specific expression ‘armed rebellion’ as a ground for proclaiming a National Emergency under Article 352.
11.tq: Test the direction of the constitutional wording change by separating the old and new expressions.
11.sec: Articles 20 and 21 during emergency - suspension status and amending act

11.s: In the context of the Supreme Court decision in Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana, reported on 14 August 2026, which of the following was emphasised?
o: The grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee
The right to education is available only to citizens
Preventive detention can be ordered only after conviction
An Advisory Board must review every arrest within 24 hours
11.x: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana emphasised that the grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee.
11.tq: Directly identify the precise legal requirement associated with a recent case.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s: Which High Court criticised routine detentions in the Chander Pal Singh case?
11.x: The Allahabad High Court criticised routine detentions in the Chander Pal Singh case.
11.tq: Use the court-case association rather than confusing similar constitutional forums.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s:
Consider the following statements regarding preventive detention in India:
1. NCRB data indicate more than 1.2 lakh preventive detentions in a year.
2. About half of these detentions have reportedly been quashed by High Courts.
3. The reported data show that preventive detention is confined to only a few dozen cases annually.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
11.x: NCRB data indicate more than 1.2 lakh preventive detentions annually, with about half reportedly quashed by High Courts. Statement 3 is false because the number is over 1.2 lakh, not a few dozen.
11.tq: Find the exaggerated numerical reversal and retain the two statements carrying the reported figures.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s: Which case is associated with shaping the right to education in the context of Andhra Pradesh?
o: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana
K.A. Najeeb v. Union of India
Harish Rana v. Union of India
Unnikrishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh
11.x: Unnikrishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh, decided in 1993, played an important role in shaping the right to education.
11.tq: Match the constitutional theme with the correct case name and State connection.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s: The criticism concerning the Forty-Fourth Amendment in the context of preventive detention is that a relevant clause remains—
o: applicable only during a financial emergency
unnotified and therefore not brought into operation
11.x: The criticism is that the relevant Forty-Fourth Amendment clause has remained unnotified and has not been brought into operation.
11.tq: Distinguish an unnotified constitutional provision from a repealed or inapplicable one.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s: Which of the following is a criticism associated with the operation of preventive detention laws?
o: Preventive detention requires a prior final conviction in every case
Preventive detention applies only to civil disputes
The expression “public order” may be used vaguely
Advisory Boards are constitutionally prohibited from reviewing detention
11.x: The vague use of the expression “public order” is a recognised criticism in debates concerning preventive detention.
11.tq: Select the legally relevant criticism and reject options that reverse the nature of preventive detention.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s: With reference to bail in cases under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, the Supreme Court has observed that delay alone is—
o: not a trump card for granting bail
sufficient to invalidate the detention order
11.x: The Supreme Court observed on 6 January 2026 that delay alone is not a “trump card” for bail in UAPA cases.
11.tq: Test the exact legal qualification instead of treating delay as an automatic remedy.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s: A letter concerning the cases of Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, citing the precedent of K.A. Najeeb, was addressed to—
o: The Chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission
11.x: The letter was addressed to Chief Justice Surya Kant and cited the K.A. Najeeb precedent in relation to Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam. It was reported on 15 August 2026.
11.tq: Identify the correct constitutional authority from a cluster of closely related legal actors.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s: Harish Rana, who had remained in a persistent vegetative state for 13 years, became the subject of proceedings concerning—
o: withdrawal of life support before the Supreme Court
enforcement of the right to education
appointment to an Advisory Board for preventive detention
11.x: In the Harish Rana matter, his parents sought withdrawal of life support before the Supreme Court after he had remained in a persistent vegetative state for 13 years.
11.tq: Apply the factual setting to identify the precise constitutional and medical-legal issue.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s: The demand to notify the relevant Forty-Fourth Amendment provision concerning preventive detention relates to limiting detention without Advisory Board confirmation to—
11.x: The demand concerns notification of the Forty-Fourth Amendment provision prescribing a two-month limit in the relevant preventive-detention context.
11.tq: Focus on the exact statutory time limit and distinguish it from familiar three- and six-month periods.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s:
Consider the following statements regarding constitutional approaches to personal liberty:
1. “Procedure established by law” is associated with Japan.
2. “Due process” is associated with the United States of America.
3. The two expressions are identified with the same constitutional system.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
11.x: “Procedure established by law” is associated with Japan, while “due process” is associated with the United States. Statement 3 is false because the expressions are associated with different constitutional systems.
11.tq: Separate the two confusable constitutional expressions by their country of association.
11.sec: Universal angles

11.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with the principal subject of the indicated constitutional Article?
o: Article 20 — protection in respect of conviction for offences
Article 21 — preventive detention and safeguards against arrest
Article 21A — protection against ex post facto criminal laws
Article 22 — compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen years
11.x: Article 20 provides protection in respect of conviction for offences. Article 21 concerns life and personal liberty, Article 21A concerns education, and Article 22 deals with protection against arrest and detention, including preventive detention safeguards.
11.tq: Use article–subject matching and eliminate options formed by swapping neighbouring Fundamental Rights.
11.sec: Universal angles

12.s: In the context of freedom of religion under the Constitution, ‘freedom of conscience’ primarily denotes:
o: The right to establish and administer religious institutions
The right to obtain state assistance for religious activities
The right to compel others to accept one's religious beliefs
The inner freedom to mould one's relation with God or creatures as one desires, including the freedom to follow no religion
12.x: Freedom of conscience concerns the inner freedom to determine one's relationship with God or creatures and also includes the freedom to follow no religion.
12.tq: Test the exact meaning of a confusable constitutional term rather than its broader subject.
12.sec: Article 25 - text of clause (1), conscience, profess, practise, propagate, limits

12.s: Which one of the following best illustrates ‘professing’ a religion under Article 25?
o: Seeking exemption from all secular regulation
Declaring one's religious beliefs openly through words or visible symbols such as a turban, crucifix or kirpan
Compelling another person to accept a religious belief
12.x: To profess religion is to declare one's beliefs openly, either verbally or through visible symbols such as a turban, crucifix or kirpan.
12.tq: Use the practical example to distinguish professing from practising and propagating.
12.sec: Article 25 - text of clause (1), conscience, profess, practise, propagate, limits

12.s: The term ‘practise’ in Article 25 is most appropriately associated with:
o: Open declaration of religious identity through symbols
Worship, rituals and ceremonies integral to a religion
The right to convert another person to one's religion
Spreading religious teachings to other persons
12.x: Practising religion includes worship, rituals and ceremonies that are integral to the religion. Open declaration is professing, while spreading beliefs is propagating.
12.tq: Split the closely related terms by matching each one with its precise constitutional meaning.
12.sec: Article 25 - text of clause (1), conscience, profess, practise, propagate, limits

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding propagation of religion under Article 25:
1. It includes spreading one's religious beliefs to others.
2. It includes an unrestricted right to convert another person.
3. A right to convert another person would affect that person's freedom of conscience.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Propagation means spreading one's beliefs, but it does not include a right to convert another person because that would impinge on the other person's freedom of conscience.
12.tq: Identify the precise limit concealed by the distinction between propagation and conversion.
12.sec: Article 25 - text of clause (1), conscience, profess, practise, propagate, limits

12.s:
Freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion under Article 25(1) are subject to which of the following?
1. Public order
2. Morality
3. Health
4. The other provisions of Part III
Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Article 25(1) expressly subjects these freedoms to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III.
12.tq: Read the complete qualifying phrase and avoid omitting the final constitutional condition.
12.sec: Article 25 - text of clause (1), conscience, profess, practise, propagate, limits

12.s: Under Article 25(2)(a), the State may regulate or restrict which of the following activities associated with religious practice?
o: Economic, financial, political or other secular activities
Only the propagation of minority religions
12.x: Article 25(2)(a) permits the State to regulate or restrict economic, financial, political or other secular activities associated with religious practice.
12.tq: Test the constitutional distinction between religious practice and associated secular activity.
12.sec: Article 25 - text of clause (1), conscience, profess, practise, propagate, limits

12.s: Which one of the following is authorised by Article 25(2)(b)?
o: Compulsory conversion of persons belonging to other religions
Provision for social welfare and reform, and throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus
State management of every private religious ceremony
12.x: Article 25(2)(b) permits social welfare and reform measures and allows Hindu religious institutions of a public character to be opened to all classes and sections of Hindus.
12.tq: Use the ‘may provide’ and ‘throw open’ powers to identify the correct constitutional exception.
12.sec: Article 25 - text of clause (1), conscience, profess, practise, propagate, limits

12.s:
Consider the following statements about the explanations attached to Article 25:
1. Wearing and carrying kirpans is deemed to be included in the profession of the Sikh religion.
2. For Article 25(2)(b), the expression ‘Hindus’ includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists.
3. The explanation relating to kirpans applies only to the practice and not to the profession of the Sikh religion.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because wearing and carrying kirpans is specifically deemed part of the profession of the Sikh religion.
12.tq: Find the wrong statement by checking the exact constitutional wording of the explanations.
12.sec: Article 25 - text of clause (1), conscience, profess, practise, propagate, limits

12.s: The Supreme Court held in Javed (2003) that polygamy is:
o: Not an essential religious practice protected by Article 25
A practice protected only for religious denominations
An essential religious practice absolutely protected by Article 25
A secular activity regulated exclusively under Article 23
12.x: In Javed (2003), polygamy was held not to be an essential religious practice protected by Article 25.
12.tq: Use the case-law name to discriminate between an essential religious practice and a non-protected practice.
12.sec: Article 25 - text of clause (1), conscience, profess, practise, propagate, limits

12.s:
Which of the following are covered by the prohibition under Article 23(1)?
1. Traffic in human beings
2. Begar
3. Other forms of forced labour
4. Compulsory service imposed for a public purpose without discrimination
Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Article 23(1) prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other forced labour. Compulsory service for a public purpose is dealt with as an exception under Article 23(2), subject to non-discrimination.
12.tq: Separate the general prohibition in clause (1) from the public-purpose exception in clause (2).
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s: ‘Begar’, as used in the context of Article 23, means:
o: Voluntary community service performed for religious purposes
Unpaid forced labour exacted by officials or zamindars
Paid labour performed under a written contract
Compulsory military service with regular remuneration
12.x: Begar refers to unpaid forced labour traditionally exacted by officials or zamindars.
12.tq: Test the exact meaning of an Indian constitutional term with a nearby but incorrect service concept.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s:
Which of the following practices are included within the forms of exploitation addressed by Article 23?
1. Sale of persons
2. Immoral traffic, including prostitution
3. Devadasi system
4. Slavery
Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: The prohibition of traffic in human beings covers sale of persons, immoral traffic including prostitution, the devadasi system and slavery.
12.tq: Use an inclusive list question to test the full scope of ‘traffic in human beings’.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s:
With reference to Article 23(2), consider the following statements:
1. The State may impose compulsory service for public purposes.
2. Such service may include military service or social service.
3. The State is required to pay remuneration in every case of compulsory service.
4. The State cannot discriminate solely on grounds of religion, race, caste or class while imposing such service.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Article 23(2) does not require payment in every case of compulsory public service, so statement 3 is false.
12.tq: Locate the exception and test it against the specific condition of non-discrimination.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s: The protection against trafficking and forced labour under Article 23 is available:
o: Only to Indian citizens and only against the State
To citizens and non-citizens, and against both the State and private persons
Only to persons employed in government institutions
Only when the exploitation is committed by a public authority
12.x: Article 23 protects both citizens and non-citizens and operates against the State as well as private persons.
12.tq: Check the scope of a fundamental right by testing both beneficiaries and enforceability against private actors.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s: Which one of the following accurately states the scope of Article 24?
o: It prohibits only unpaid employment of children below 14 years.
It prohibits employment of a child below 14 years in any factory, mine or other hazardous employment.
It prohibits employment of children below 14 years in all forms of harmless household work.
It prohibits every form of work by every person below 18 years of age.
12.x: Article 24 prohibits employment of a child below 14 years in a factory, mine or other hazardous employment. It does not bar harmless or innocent work.
12.tq: Avoid the extreme-word trap by distinguishing hazardous employment from all forms of work.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s: Which pair most directly strengthens the constitutional protection of children against exploitation by combining education and child-labour safeguards?
12.x: Article 21A provides free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 years, while Article 24 prohibits their employment in factories, mines and hazardous work. Together they make the right against exploitation more meaningful for children.
12.tq: Link the complementary provisions instead of treating each Article in isolation.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s: The constitutional guarantee under Article 21A relates to free and compulsory education for children in which age group?
12.x: Article 21A concerns free and compulsory education for children from 6 to 14 years of age.
12.tq: Discriminate between the age range for education and the age threshold for hazardous employment.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the offence of trafficking is presently dealt with under:
12.x: Trafficking is dealt with under Section 143 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. It replaced Section 370 of the Indian Penal Code for this offence.
12.tq: Use the changed statutory provision as a current-affairs legal trap against the former IPC section.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s: In determining the offence of trafficking under the applicable criminal law, the consent of the victim is:
o: Relevant only when no monetary consideration is involved
Relevant only when the victim is an adult
12.x: The victim's consent is immaterial for determining the offence of trafficking.
12.tq: Test the legal consequence of consent by rejecting qualifications not supported by the rule.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
 a. Article 24
 b. Article 25
 c. Article 26
 d. Article 27

List-II (Subject)
 i. Freedom to manage religious affairs
 ii. Freedom from taxes for promotion of a particular religion
 iii. Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
 iv. Prohibition of employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines and hazardous work

Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Article 24 concerns child labour; Article 25 concerns freedom of conscience and religious practice; Article 26 concerns management of religious affairs; and Article 27 concerns freedom from taxes for promoting a particular religion.
12.tq: Start from the sure Article–subject pairs and eliminate codes containing a misplaced religious freedom.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
 a. Article 24
 b. Article 25
 c. Article 27
 d. Article 28

List-II (Right or freedom)
 i. Freedom from attending religious instruction or worship in certain institutions
 ii. Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
 iii. Prohibition of employment of children below 14 years in hazardous employment
 iv. Freedom from taxes for promotion of a particular religion

Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: The correct pairing is Article 24–child labour, Article 25–freedom of religion, Article 27–freedom from religious promotion taxes and Article 28–freedom concerning religious instruction or worship in certain institutions.
12.tq: Use the sequential Article range while checking each subject against its exact constitutional guarantee.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Judgment in Javed concerning polygamy and Article 25
B. Enactment of the 86th Constitutional Amendment
C. Enactment of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
D. Coming into force of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita

Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: The correct sequence is the Javed judgment in 2003, the 86th Amendment in 2002? No—the amendment predates the judgment. Therefore the correct chronological order is B (2002), A (2003), C (2023), D (1 July 2024).
12.tq: Anchor the sequence with the dated constitutional amendment before the 2003 judgment, then place the 2023 law and its 2024 commencement.
12.sec: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

12.s: The Right to Freedom of Religion guaranteed under Articles 25 to 28 of the Constitution is classified as a:
12.x: The freedoms guaranteed under Articles 25 to 28 constitute Fundamental Rights and are not merely legal rights or Directive Principles.
12.tq: Test the constitutional classification directly and distinguish a Fundamental Right from a legal right or DPSP.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s:
Consider the following pairs regarding the availability of rights:
1. Article 25 — All persons
2. Article 26 — Religious denominations or any section thereof
3. Article 27 — Citizens only
4. Article 28 — All persons
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
12.x: Articles 25, 27 and 28 are available to all persons, including citizens and foreigners. Article 26 is available to religious denominations or any section thereof; therefore, pair 3 is incorrect.
12.tq: Use the comparison table and identify the swapped eligibility category.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s: Which one of the following rights under the freedom of religion is available specifically to religious denominations or any section thereof?
o: Freedom from religious instruction in State-funded institutions under Article 28
Freedom to manage religious affairs under Article 26
Freedom from taxation for promotion of a religion under Article 27
12.x: Article 26 is available to religious denominations or any section thereof. Articles 25, 27 and 28 are available to all persons.
12.tq: Discriminate between the similarly grouped Articles 25 to 28 by matching the right with its beneficiaries.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s:
Freedom of religion under Articles 25 to 28 is subject to which of the following limitations?
1. Public order
2. Morality
3. Health
4. The rights guaranteed under Part III, in the case of Article 25
Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: The freedom of religion is subject to public order, morality and health. Article 25 is additionally subject to the other provisions of Part III.
12.tq: Check the full set of constitutional limitations rather than stopping at the three common restrictions.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s: A State law seeks to remove a social evil associated with a religious practice. Which constitutional position is most appropriate?
o: The State may intervene to root out social evils, subject to constitutional limitations.
Only Parliament can intervene in every religious practice.
Such intervention is valid only if the practice is followed by foreigners.
The State can never intervene in religious matters.
12.x: Freedom of religion is not absolute. The State can intervene to root out social evils, while respecting the applicable constitutional restrictions.
12.tq: Apply the non-absolute nature of religious freedom to a short constitutional scenario.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s: The Essential Religious Practice test is best described as a test used by courts to determine:
o: Whether a practice is integral to a religion and therefore protected
Whether a religion has received State recognition
Whether a person is eligible to vote in a religious institution
Whether a religious institution is wholly funded by the State
12.x: The Essential Religious Practice test is a court-made test for deciding whether a practice is integral to a religion and consequently protected. The Constitution itself does not define the expression “essential”.
12.tq: Test the exact meaning of a judicial doctrine rather than its name alone.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s:
With reference to the Essential Religious Practice test, consider the following statements:
1. It was formulated by the Supreme Court in 1954.
2. The Constitution expressly defines the term “essential” in relation to religious practices.
3. It is used to identify practices integral to a religion.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: The doctrine was formulated by the Supreme Court in 1954 and concerns practices integral to a religion. The Constitution does not define “essential”; statement 2 is false.
12.tq: Use a precise constitutional-versus-judicial distinction to reject the false statement.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Article 27?
o: It permits taxation exclusively for a religion followed by the majority.
It guarantees the right of every denomination to own property.
It prohibits religious instruction in every educational institution.
It prohibits taxation specifically for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion.
12.x: Article 27 embodies the neutrality principle that no person can be compelled to pay a tax specifically appropriated for the promotion or maintenance of a particular religion.
12.tq: Match the Article with its precise neutrality provision and avoid swapping it with Articles 26 or 28.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s: Under Article 28(1), religious instruction is prohibited in:
o: Only institutions receiving foreign financial assistance
Every institution administered by a religious denomination
All private educational institutions without exception
Educational institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
12.x: Article 28(1) prohibits religious instruction in educational institutions wholly maintained out of State funds.
12.tq: Focus on the exact funding condition rather than extending the prohibition to all institutions.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s: Which of the following statements correctly reflects the constitutional position regarding conversion?
o: Conversion can be regulated only by religious denominations and not by the State.
Forcible conversion is not protected as a part of freedom of religion.
The Constitution expressly guarantees forcible conversion as part of religious freedom.
The right to propagate religion includes an unrestricted right to convert another person.
12.x: Freedom to propagate religion does not include forcible conversion. The State may regulate activities involving coercion and social harm.
12.tq: Reject the extreme interpretation that converts propagation into an unrestricted power to convert.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s:
Which of the following pairs of anti-conversion laws and years is correctly matched?
1. Orissa Freedom of Religion Act — 1967
2. Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam — 1968
12.x: The Orissa Freedom of Religion Act was enacted in 1967, while the Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam was enacted in 1968.
12.tq: Use the year-pair method to distinguish two similarly named State anti-conversion laws.
12.sec: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health  [APPSC]

12.s: Which one of the following cases is associated with the origin of the Essential Religious Practice doctrine?
o: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala
Shayara Bano v. Union of India
Rev. Stanislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh
12.x: The Shirur Mutt case, formally Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v. Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, in 1954 is associated with the origin of the Essential Religious Practice doctrine.
12.tq: Recall the landmark case linked to the origin of a doctrine, not merely its later applications.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Case)
a. Shirur Mutt case
b. Rev. Stanislaus case
c. Bijoe Emmanuel case
 d. Shayara Bano case

List-II (Issue or holding)
i. Jehovah’s Witness children and the National Anthem
 ii. Instant triple talaq
 iii. Essential Religious Practice doctrine
 iv. Right to propagate does not include right to convert

Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Shirur Mutt is associated with the ERP doctrine; Rev. Stanislaus with propagation and conversion; Bijoe Emmanuel with the National Anthem; and Shayara Bano with instant triple talaq.
12.tq: Start from the sure case-issue pairs and eliminate codes that reverse the landmark holdings.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s: The Supreme Court’s decision in Rev. Stanislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1977) held that:
o: The right to propagate includes an absolute right to convert.
The right to propagate does not include a right to convert, and upheld specified anti-conversion Acts.
Women of all ages must be permitted entry into Sabarimala.
12.x: The Court held that the right to propagate religion does not include the right to convert another person and upheld the Orissa and Madhya Pradesh anti-conversion Acts.
12.tq: Use the case-year-issue combination and guard against swapping holdings between religion cases.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Shayara Bano v. Union of India
B. Shirur Mutt case
C. Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala
D. Rev. Stanislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh
12.x: The cases were decided in the order Shirur Mutt (1954), Rev. Stanislaus (1977), Bijoe Emmanuel (1986), and Shayara Bano (2017).
12.tq: Place the earliest and latest cases first, then distinguish the two middle dates.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s: In Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986), the Supreme Court held that Jehovah’s Witness children:
o: Were exempt from attending educational institutions.
Could refuse to stand during the National Anthem as an absolute religious right.
Could be compelled to sing the National Anthem if they stood in the assembly.
Could not be compelled to sing the National Anthem and that standing respectfully was sufficient.
12.x: The Court held that the children could not be compelled to sing the National Anthem; standing respectfully was considered sufficient.
12.tq: Test the precise distinction between non-singing and disrespectful conduct.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s: Which one of the following was NOT left open by the judgment in Shayara Bano v. Union of India?
o: The broader question of certain personal-law practices
12.x: The judgment invalidated instant triple talaq. Polygamy and nikah halala were left open for consideration.
12.tq: Find the one issue decided by the judgment among issues expressly left open.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s:
With reference to the Sabarimala judgment, consider the following statements:
1. Women of all ages were allowed entry.
2. The Court held that devotion cannot be subjected to gender discrimination.
3. The exclusion of women was accepted as an Essential Religious Practice.
4. Secularism was reaffirmed as part of the Basic Structure.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: The Sabarimala judgment allowed women of all ages, rejected gender discrimination in devotion and reaffirmed secularism as part of the Basic Structure. The exclusion was not accepted as an ERP, making statement 3 false.
12.tq: Identify the single reversed holding in a group of closely related case propositions.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s: The Sabarimala judgment of 28 September 2018 was delivered by:
o: A three-judge Bench with a unanimous decision
A seven-judge Bench with a 5:2 decision
A nine-judge Bench with a unanimous decision
A five-judge Bench with a 4:1 decision
12.x: The Sabarimala judgment was delivered by a five-judge Bench in a 4:1 decision on 28 September 2018.
12.tq: Test the Bench strength, voting ratio and date as a combined judicial fact.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Sabarimala case is correct?
o: Ayyappa devotees were not held to be a separate religious denomination, and exclusion was not accepted as an ERP.
Ayyappa devotees were held to be a separate religious denomination and exclusion was declared an ERP.
The judgment dealt exclusively with instant triple talaq.
The Court held that secularism is not part of the Basic Structure.
12.x: The Sabarimala decision held that Ayyappa devotees did not constitute a separate religious denomination for this purpose and that the exclusion was not an Essential Religious Practice.
12.tq: Use the case-specific identity and ERP findings to reject swapped holdings.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s: Who were the first women of the barred age group reported to have entered the Sabarimala temple in January 2019?
o: Kanaka Durga and Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar
12.x: Bindu Ammini and Kanaka Durga were reported as the first women of the barred age group to enter Sabarimala in January 2019.
12.tq: Recall the paired names associated with the immediate aftermath of a landmark judgment.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s: The review reference concerning the Essential Religious Practice doctrine across faiths was heard by a nine-judge Constitution Bench headed by:
12.x: The nine-judge Constitution Bench hearing the reference was headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant.
12.tq: Distinguish the head of the judicial Bench from the counsel appearing before it.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s: Which of the following represents the Centre’s argument in the 2026 Sabarimala reference proceedings?
o: Only practices proved to be essential are protected under religious freedom.
Religious practices are protected only when approved by Parliament.
Protection is not limited to essential practices; every practice is protected unless it breaches public order, morality or health, with the burden on the challenger.
The State can prohibit every practice without constitutional scrutiny.
12.x: The Centre argued that protection is not confined to essential practices and that every practice is protected unless it breaches public order, morality or health; it also placed the burden on the challenger.
12.tq: Separate a party’s argument in pending proceedings from the final holding of an earlier case.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s: Which one of the following correctly states the Karnataka High Court position on the hijab in 2022?
o: Hijab was held to be an Essential Religious Practice.
Hijab was declared part of the Basic Structure.
Hijab was held not to be an Essential Religious Practice.
Hijab was held identical to carrying a kirpan under Article 25.
12.x: The Karnataka High Court held in 2022 that hijab was not an Essential Religious Practice. The Allahabad High Court relied on this position in August 2026 while rejecting a schoolgirl’s plea.
12.tq: Test the exact court and holding without confusing hijab with the kirpan explanation.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s: Which of the following is NOT a right of a religious denomination under Article 26, subject to public order, morality and health?
o: To establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes
To impose a compulsory tax on every person for its religious purposes
To manage its own affairs in matters of religion
12.x: Article 26 includes the rights to establish and maintain institutions, manage religious affairs, own and acquire property, and administer property in accordance with law. It does not confer a power to impose compulsory taxes on everyone.
12.tq: Find the option that is a coercive financial power rather than one of the four Article 26 rights.
12.sec: Religion cases → issue  [APPSC]

12.s:
For the purposes of Article 25(2)(b), the expression “Hindus” includes persons professing which of the following religions?
1. Sikhism
2. Jainism
3. Buddhism
Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Explanation II to Article 25(2)(b) provides that “Hindus” includes persons professing the Sikh, Jaina or Buddhist religion. Hindu religious institutions are construed accordingly.
12.tq: Test the complete inclusive list and avoid treating “Hindus” as confined to one faith.
12.sec: Explanations to Article 25 - kirpan; "Hindus"  [other exams]

12.s: Explanation II to Article 25(2)(b) is also relevant because Hindu religious institutions are:
o: Construed accordingly for the purposes of the provision
Restricted to institutions serving only foreign citizens
Placed outside the scope of Article 25
12.x: Explanation II states that the reference to Hindus includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists, and that Hindu religious institutions are construed accordingly.
12.tq: Test the consequence attached to an Explanation rather than only memorising its listed religions.
12.sec: Explanations to Article 25 - kirpan; "Hindus"  [other exams]

12.s: Which one of the following Acts specifically penalises brothels, pimping and living off the earnings of prostitution?
o: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
12.x: The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 penalises brothels, pimping and living off another person’s earnings from prostitution.
12.tq: Use the scope of the statute to distinguish it from neighbouring labour and child-protection laws.
12.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

12.s: The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 is primarily concerned with the abolition of
12.x: The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 abolishes bonded labour, including debt bondage found in sectors such as brick kilns, agriculture and domestic work.
12.tq: Match the statute with its precise subject rather than with a related constitutional article.
12.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

12.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act — 1956
2. Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act — 1976
3. Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act — 1986
4. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — 2023
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
12.x: All four pairs are correctly matched. The respective years are 1956, 1976, 1986 and 2023.
12.tq: Verify each year independently before selecting the coded combination.
12.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

12.s: The 2016 amendment to the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act provided that
o: no person below eighteen years may work in any occupation
children below twelve years may work in non-hazardous factories
only bonded labour by children was prohibited
no child below fourteen years may work in any occupation, while adolescents aged fourteen to eighteen may not work in hazardous occupations
12.x: The 2016 amendment prohibited employment of children below fourteen years in any occupation and prohibited adolescents aged fourteen to eighteen from hazardous work.
12.tq: Separate the two age bands and their different prohibitions.
12.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

12.s:
With reference to trafficking under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, consider the following statements:
1. Trafficking is dealt with under Section 143.
2. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code from 1 July 2024.
3. The consent of a victim is immaterial for determining the trafficking offence.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: All three statements are correct: Section 143 addresses trafficking, the BNS replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024, and victim consent does not validate trafficking.
12.tq: Check the section number, commencement date and legal effect of consent as separate details.
12.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

12.s: Which of the following is associated with the institutional response to human trafficking?
o: District Anti-Human Trafficking Units funded by the Ministry of Home Affairs
State Finance Commissions funded by the Election Commission
District Legal Services Authorities funded by the Reserve Bank of India
National Human Rights Courts funded by the Ministry of Education
12.x: District Anti-Human Trafficking Units are associated with the response to trafficking and are funded by the Ministry of Home Affairs. The POCSO Act, 2012 is also a linked child-protection law.
12.tq: Identify the correct ministry-body association and reject swapped institutional authorities.
12.sec: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

12.s: Which one of the following rights is available to every religious denomination or any section thereof, subject to public order, morality and health?
o: The right to exempt all property from regulation by law
The right to compel religious instruction in every school
The right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion
The right to impose a tax for religious purposes
12.x: Article 26 gives every religious denomination or section thereof the right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion, subject to public order, morality and health.
12.tq: Ask who holds the right and then apply the constitutional limitations.
12.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

12.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 26:
1. A religious denomination may establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes.
2. It may own and acquire movable and immovable property.
3. It may administer its property in accordance with law.
4. These rights are subject to public order, morality and health.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: Article 26 includes all four rights and expressly subjects them to public order, morality and health.
12.tq: Test the complete set of clauses and the common constitutional limitations together.
12.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

12.s: Article 27 prohibits
o: every fee imposed by a public authority in connection with a religious institution
compelling a person to pay taxes, the proceeds of which are specifically used to promote a particular religion
all public expenditure benefiting religious communities equally
the State from regulating secular administration of religious institutions
12.x: Article 27 bars compulsory payment of taxes whose proceeds are used to promote a particular religion. It does not bar all fees or expenditure benefiting all religions equally.
12.tq: Distinguish a tax from a fee and a particular-religion purpose from equal public support.
12.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

12.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Article 27 is correct?
o: Taxes may be collected only for the promotion of the majority religion.
A fee for the secular administration of a religious institution is permissible.
Article 27 applies only to religious denominations and not to individuals.
Every fee connected with a religious institution is unconstitutional.
12.x: Article 27 bars taxes for promoting a particular religion, but a fee imposed for secular administration of a religious institution is permissible.
12.tq: Find the precise exception instead of treating the constitutional prohibition as absolute.
12.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

12.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
(a) Article 26
(b) Article 27
(c) Article 28(1)
(d) Article 28(3)

List-II (Subject)
(i) No person compelled to attend religious instruction without consent
(ii) Religious denomination’s right to manage religious affairs
(iii) No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
(iv) No compulsory tax for promotion of a particular religion

Select the correct answer using the code below.
12.x: Article 26 concerns denominational religious affairs; Article 27 concerns taxes; Article 28(1) concerns State-funded religious instruction; and Article 28(3) protects freedom from compulsory attendance.
12.tq: Start with the sure Article 27 pair and then complete the Article 28 distinctions.
12.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

12.s: A State-administered educational institution was established under a trust or endowment that requires religious instruction. Under Article 28, such instruction is
o: permitted because the institution is administered by the State and the trust requires it
permitted only if every student belongs to the same religion
permitted only in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
12.x: Article 28(2) does not apply the prohibition to a State-administered institution established under an endowment or trust requiring religious instruction.
12.tq: Apply the trust/endowment exception rather than relying only on the institution’s State administration.
12.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

12.s: In a State-recognised or State-aided educational institution, attendance at religious instruction
o: is prohibited even when the student and guardian consent
may be compelled by the head of the institution
cannot be compelled without the individual’s consent; in the case of a minor, the guardian’s consent is required
is compulsory if the institution receives State aid
12.x: Article 28(3) prevents compulsion to attend religious instruction in State-recognised or aided institutions. For a minor, the guardian’s consent is required.
12.tq: Track the difference between prohibition of instruction and prohibition of compulsory attendance.
12.sec: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

12.s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam
B. Orissa Freedom of Religion Act
C. Stanislaus decision upholding such laws
D. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita coming into force in place of the IPC
12.x: The Orissa Act was enacted in 1967, the Madhya Pradesh law in 1968, Stanislaus was decided in 1977, and the BNS replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024.
12.tq: Fix the two adjacent enactment years first, then place the judgment and the BNS.
12.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

12.s: The Orissa Freedom of Religion Act, 1967 and the Madhya Pradesh Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam, 1968 were initially enacted primarily in response to concerns about
o: sacrilege of the Guru Granth Sahib
12.x: Both early State laws arose from concerns over missionary activity. Later amendments widened their scope to conversions to Islam as well.
12.tq: Identify the original policy concern and distinguish it from later amendments.
12.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

12.s: Which one of the following best describes the significance of the Stanislaus v. Madhya Pradesh decision, 1977?
o: It prohibited every form of religious propagation.
It declared all State conversion laws unconstitutional.
It held that propagation necessarily includes a right to convert another person by force.
It upheld State conversion laws and held that propagation does not include forcible conversion.
12.x: In Stanislaus v. Madhya Pradesh, 1977, such State laws were upheld and propagation was held not to include forcible conversion.
12.tq: Separate propagation from forcible conversion, the central conceptual distinction in the case.
12.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

12.s: The later amendments to certain State freedom-of-religion laws widened their scope from concerns over Christian missionary activity to include conversions to
12.x: The later amendments widened the scope of the laws to cover conversions to Islam in addition to the earlier concern over Christian missionary activity.
12.tq: Test the specific expansion of scope rather than the general existence of conversion laws.
12.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

12.s: Section 295A of the Indian Penal Code, concerning deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings, was upheld in
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Ramji Lal Modi v. State of Uttar Pradesh
12.x: Ramji Lal Modi v. State of Uttar Pradesh upheld Section 295A on public-order grounds. The corresponding provision is now Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
12.tq: Match the case with the statutory provision and its constitutional ground.
12.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

12.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Section 295A of the IPC is now reflected as Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
2. The provision concerns deliberate outrage of religious feelings.
3. It was upheld in Ramji Lal Modi v. State of Uttar Pradesh on public-order grounds.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
12.x: All three statements are correct. Section 299 of the BNS corresponds to the earlier Section 295A, which was upheld in Ramji Lal Modi on public-order grounds.
12.tq: Combine the old provision, new provision and leading case instead of confusing the two section numbers.
12.sec: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

12.s: The Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act, which received assent in April 2026, is associated with
o: compulsory religious instruction in Punjab schools
removal of Article 27 restrictions on religious taxes
abolition of all State conversion laws in Punjab
a maximum punishment of life imprisonment for sacrilege of the Guru Granth Sahib
12.x: The Punjab amendment allows punishment of up to life imprisonment for sacrilege of the Guru Granth Sahib. It has been challenged before the Punjab and Haryana High Court on the ground that it protects only one faith.
