25.tq: Identify the one statement that wrongly substitutes declaration of result for assumption of office.
25.sec: Vacancy - election time limit and acting President  [APPSC]

25.s: When the Vice-President acts as President under Article 65, which one of the following is correct?
o: The Vice-President continues to preside over the Rajya Sabha while acting as President
The Deputy Chairman presides over the Rajya Sabha during that period
The Rajya Sabha is automatically dissolved
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over the Rajya Sabha
25.x: While acting as President, the Vice-President ceases to perform the functions of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; the Deputy Chairman presides.
25.tq: Use the role-separation trap: a person acting as President cannot simultaneously perform the Chairman’s functions in the Rajya Sabha.
25.sec: Vacancy - election time limit and acting President  [APPSC]

25.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a vacancy in the office of the Vice-President from a vacancy in the office of the President?
o: A Vice-Presidential vacancy is filled only by nomination
A Vice-Presidential vacancy must also be filled within six months
A Vice-Presidential vacancy cannot arise by resignation
A Vice-Presidential vacancy has no six-month deadline under Article 68
25.x: Unlike a casual vacancy in the office of the President, Article 68 does not prescribe a six-month deadline for filling a Vice-Presidential vacancy.
25.tq: Discriminate between the similar-looking vacancy provisions of Articles 62 and 68.
25.sec: Vacancy - election time limit and acting President  [APPSC]

25.s: If the offices of both the President and Vice-President are vacant, who acts as President first?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
25.x: When both offices are vacant, the Chief Justice of India acts as President; in the absence of the CJI, the senior-most Supreme Court judge performs the function.
25.tq: Test the constitutional succession sequence by identifying the first office-holder in the chain.
25.sec: Vacancy - election time limit and acting President  [APPSC]

25.s: All doubts and disputes relating to the election of the President or Vice-President are decided by:
25.x: Article 71 vests the Supreme Court with exclusive authority to decide doubts and disputes concerning Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections.
25.tq: Use the authority-identification method: distinguish the body conducting an election from the body deciding its disputes.
25.sec: Election disputes - Article 71  [other exams]

25.s:
With reference to Article 71, consider the following statements:
1. The Supreme Court alone decides disputes concerning the election of the President and Vice-President.
2. Parliament may regulate matters connected with such elections other than the adjudication of election disputes.
3. An election can be challenged merely because there is a vacancy in the electoral college.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because Article 71(4) bars a challenge on the ground of a vacancy in the electoral college.
25.tq: Find the exception hidden in the negative statement about vacancies in the electoral college.
25.sec: Election disputes - Article 71  [other exams]

25.s: The 39th Constitutional Amendment and the 44th Constitutional Amendment had what effect on Presidential election disputes?
o: The 39th Amendment vested the disputes in Parliament and the 44th retained that arrangement
The 39th Amendment removed the Supreme Court’s power and the 44th Amendment restored it
The 39th Amendment created the power and the 44th Amendment abolished it
Both Amendments transferred the power to the Election Commission
25.x: The 39th Amendment of 1975 took away the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction over these disputes, while the 44th Amendment of 1978 restored it.
25.tq: Link each Amendment to its opposite constitutional effect instead of relying on the later amendment alone.
25.sec: Election disputes - Article 71  [other exams]

25.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Zakir Husain — First President from South India
Rajendra Prasad — Only President elected twice
S. Radhakrishnan — First President to die in office
M. Hidayatullah — Only President elected unopposed
25.x: Rajendra Prasad was the only President elected twice, in 1952 and 1957. Radhakrishnan was the first President from South India, Zakir Husain was the first to die in office, and Hidayatullah acted as President.
25.tq: Use the wrong-person-with-deed trap by matching each President with the correct distinction.
25.sec: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs  [other exams]

25.s: Who was the first President of India from South India and had earlier served as the first Vice-President?
25.x: S. Radhakrishnan, President from 1962 to 1967, was the first President from South India and had earlier been the first Vice-President.
25.tq: Combine two linked identifiers to distinguish a President from other holders of ‘first’ positions.
25.sec: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs  [other exams]

25.s: Who was the first President of India to die in office?
25.x: Zakir Husain, who served from 1967 to 1969, was the first President of India to die in office.
25.tq: Test the exact sequence of similar facts concerning Presidents who died while holding office.
25.sec: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs  [other exams]

25.s: M. Hidayatullah is remembered in the constitutional history of India as the:
o: Only Chief Justice of India to act as President
25.x: M. Hidayatullah was the only Chief Justice of India to act as President.
25.tq: Identify the unique institutional combination rather than confusing an acting President with an elected President.
25.sec: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs  [other exams]

25.s: V.V. Giri became President after winning on the basis of:
o: A nomination by the Supreme Court
25.x: V.V. Giri won the 1969 Presidential election on second-preference votes.
25.tq: Test the distinctive election feature attached to the individual President.
25.sec: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs  [other exams]

25.s: Who acted as President after the death of Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed?
25.x: After Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed died in office, B.D. Jatti acted as President.
25.tq: Avoid the chronology trap by separating the President who died in office from the person who acted afterward.
25.sec: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs  [other exams]

25.s:
Consider the following statements about N. Sanjiva Reddy:
1. He was the only President elected unopposed.
2. He was from Andhra Pradesh.
3. He had earlier served as Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
4. He was the first Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: All four statements correctly describe N. Sanjiva Reddy, who served as President from 1977 to 1982.
25.tq: Use the all-inclusive option only after verifying each biographical identifier separately.
25.sec: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs  [other exams]

25.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
25.x: Rajendra Prasad was the first President of India and the only President elected twice; Pratibha Patil was the first woman President.
25.tq: Find the biography attached to the wrong President, a standard wrong-person-with-deed trap.
25.sec: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs  [other exams]

25.s:
Arrange the following Presidents of India in chronological order of assuming office:
A. K.R. Narayanan
B. Pratibha Patil
C. N. Sanjiva Reddy
D. Droupadi Murmu
25.x: N. Sanjiva Reddy assumed office in 1977, K.R. Narayanan in 1997, Pratibha Patil in 2007 and Droupadi Murmu in 2022.
25.tq: Place the earliest and latest office-holders first, then resolve the two middle dates.
25.sec: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs  [other exams]

25.s: Droupadi Murmu assumed office as the President of India on:
25.x: Droupadi Murmu became President on 25 July 2022 and is the first tribal President of India.
25.tq: Test the exact year associated with a recent constitutional office-holder rather than the sequence number alone.
25.sec: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs  [other exams]

25.s: Which of the following forms of clemency removes both the sentence and the conviction?
25.x: A pardon removes the sentence as well as the conviction. Commutation substitutes a lighter punishment, remission reduces the period, and reprieve temporarily stays execution.
25.tq: Discriminate among closely related forms of pardoning power by their legal effect.
25.sec: Pardoning power - Article 72 vs 161  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with its meaning?
o: Remission — reduction of the period of sentence without changing its character
Respite — removal of conviction and sentence
Reprieve — substitution of a lighter form of punishment
25.x: Remission reduces the period of punishment while retaining its character. Reprieve is a temporary stay, commutation substitutes a lighter punishment, and pardon removes conviction and sentence.
25.tq: Start from the precise meaning of one form and eliminate the swapped meanings of the other forms.
25.sec: Pardoning power - Article 72 vs 161  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the pardoning powers of the President and Governor:
1. The President may pardon a death sentence.
2. The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence but may suspend, remit or commute it.
3. The Governor may grant pardon in a court-martial case.
4. The President may exercise pardoning power in court-martial cases.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the Governor has no power to pardon a court-martial sentence.
25.tq: Separate the President’s wider jurisdiction over death sentences and court-martial cases from the Governor’s narrower power.
25.sec: Pardoning power - Article 72 vs 161  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: The pardoning power of the President under Article 72 and of the Governor under Article 161 respectively relates primarily to offences against:
25.x: The President deals with offences against Union laws, while the Governor deals with offences against State laws.
25.tq: Use the Union–State jurisdiction contrast to avoid reversing the two constitutional provisions.
25.sec: Pardoning power - Article 72 vs 161  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: The pardoning power of the President is exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers according to:
o: Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh (2006)
25.x: Maru Ram (1980) established that the President exercises the pardoning power on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
25.tq: Match the case with its specific constitutional holding rather than grouping all pardon cases together.
25.sec: Pardoning power - Article 72 vs 161  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: Which one of the following correctly states the scope of judicial review of the President’s pardoning power?
o: It may be reviewed only for violation of a fundamental right expressly named in the order
It is completely immune from judicial review
It may be reviewed for mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant grounds
It can be reviewed only by Parliament
25.x: Kehar Singh and Epuru Sudhakar recognised limited judicial review where the exercise is mala fide, arbitrary or based on irrelevant grounds.
25.tq: Reject the extreme-word trap in ‘completely immune’ and apply the limited-review principle.
25.sec: Pardoning power - Article 72 vs 161  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: An Ordinance under Article 123 may be promulgated by the President only when:
o: Either House of Parliament is not in session and immediate action is considered necessary
The Lok Sabha alone has been dissolved permanently
The Supreme Court directs the President to promulgate it
Both Houses of Parliament are in session and urgent legislation is required
25.x: Article 123 permits an Ordinance when Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied that immediate action is necessary. The expression includes a situation in which either House is not in session.
25.tq: Focus on the exact constitutional condition and avoid the trap that both Houses must be absent simultaneously.
25.sec: Ordinance - Article 123, life, lapse, review cases  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: An Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 has the same force and effect as:
o: A resolution of either House of Parliament
An executive order of the Prime Minister
25.x: An Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, subject to the constitutional limits governing its promulgation and duration.
25.tq: Distinguish legal force from constitutional status: an Ordinance is not a constitutional amendment.
25.sec: Ordinance - Article 123, life, lapse, review cases  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: An Ordinance promulgated by the President ceases to operate:
o: Six weeks after Parliament reassembles, unless earlier disapproved by both Houses
Six months after promulgation in every case
Only when the President withdraws it
Six weeks after it is promulgated, irrespective of Parliament’s sittings
25.x: An Ordinance lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles, or earlier if both Houses disapprove it. The President may also withdraw it at any time.
25.tq: Combine the normal lapse rule with the earlier-disapproval exception instead of using the maximum-life figure alone.
25.sec: Ordinance - Article 123, life, lapse, review cases  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: What is the maximum possible life of a Presidential Ordinance, assuming the constitutional conditions for its promulgation and continuation are met?
25.x: The maximum possible life of an Ordinance is six months plus six weeks, linked to the interval between parliamentary sessions and the post-reassembly period.
25.tq: Do not confuse the six-week post-reassembly period with the total maximum life.
25.sec: Ordinance - Article 123, life, lapse, review cases  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: Which one of the following statements about the legislative scope of a Presidential Ordinance is correct?
o: It may amend the Constitution because it has the force of an Act
Its scope is co-extensive with Parliament’s legislative power and it cannot amend the Constitution
It may legislate on any matter, including matters beyond Parliament’s competence
It can be issued only on State List subjects
25.x: An Ordinance can cover matters within Parliament’s legislative competence, but it cannot be used to amend the Constitution.
25.tq: Separate the scope of ordinary legislation from the higher power of constitutional amendment.
25.sec: Ordinance - Article 123, life, lapse, review cases  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: The Governor’s power corresponding to the President’s power to promulgate Ordinances under Article 123 is provided under:
25.x: Article 213 confers the parallel Ordinance-making power on the Governor of a State.
25.tq: Discriminate between the Governor’s pardoning provision and the Governor’s Ordinance provision.
25.sec: Ordinance - Article 123, life, lapse, review cases  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: Which Constitutional Amendment made the President’s satisfaction in promulgating an Ordinance final, and which Amendment reversed that position?
o: 38th Amendment made it final; 44th Amendment reversed it
39th Amendment made it final; 42nd Amendment reversed it
42nd Amendment made it final; 44th Amendment reversed it
44th Amendment made it final; 38th Amendment reversed it
25.x: The 38th Amendment of 1975 made the President’s satisfaction final, while the 44th Amendment reversed that position.
25.tq: Pair the two Amendments with opposite effects and check their chronological order.
25.sec: Ordinance - Article 123, life, lapse, review cases  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: The Supreme Court in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) held that:
o: Every Ordinance automatically becomes a constitutional amendment
Routine re-promulgation of Ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution
The President’s satisfaction is never subject to review
An Ordinance must remain in force for at least six months
25.x: D.C. Wadhwa held that routine re-promulgation without placing the Ordinance before the legislature amounts to a fraud on the Constitution.
25.tq: Match the case with its distinctive holding and avoid importing the later case’s broader formulation.
25.sec: Ordinance - Article 123, life, lapse, review cases  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: Which of the following was held in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017)?
o: The Ordinance-making power was held to be a power to amend the Constitution
Re-promulgation is always valid if the executive considers it necessary
A seven-judge Bench held re-promulgation unconstitutional, made laying before the House mandatory and treated satisfaction as justiciable
The President alone may decide whether an Ordinance should be laid before the House
25.x: The seven-judge Bench in Krishna Kumar Singh held that re-promulgation is unconstitutional, laying the Ordinance before the House is mandatory, and the satisfaction is justiciable.
25.tq: Use the case-name-to-holding method and identify the option containing all three linked holdings.
25.sec: Ordinance - Article 123, life, lapse, review cases  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the absolute veto of the President of India?
o: Keeping a Bill pending without deciding on it
Returning an Ordinary Bill for reconsideration once
Overriding a Bill by a higher majority in Parliament
25.x: Absolute veto means withholding assent to a Bill. It may apply to Private Members’ Bills and Government Bills when the Council of Ministers has resigned before assent.
25.tq: Distinguish the three forms of presidential veto by their operative effect: withhold, return or keep pending.
25.sec: ■ Veto types → Bills  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: The absolute veto of the President may ordinarily be exercised in respect of which of the following?
o: Private Members’ Bills and Government Bills when the Cabinet has resigned before assent
Bills passed by a State Legislature only
25.x: The absolute veto involves withholding assent and is relevant to Private Members’ Bills and Government Bills when the Cabinet resigns before assent.
25.tq: Match the veto with the specific class of Bills to which it applies, while rejecting extreme alternatives such as ‘alone’.
25.sec: ■ Veto types → Bills  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the suspensive veto of the President:
1. It involves returning a Bill for reconsideration once.
2. If the Bill is passed again, the President must give assent.
3. It is available in respect of Money Bills.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: A suspensive veto permits the President to return an Ordinary Bill once for reconsideration. If Parliament passes it again, assent becomes mandatory. This veto does not apply to Money Bills.
25.tq: Find the single wrong statement by testing the important Money Bill exception.
25.sec: ■ Veto types → Bills  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: With reference to the pocket veto of the President of India, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It can be exercised only for a period of six months.
It permits the President to return a Money Bill for reconsideration.
It keeps an Ordinary Bill pending without any constitutional time limit for decision.
It is a veto that can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Parliament.
25.x: Pocket veto means keeping a Bill pending without taking a decision. The Constitution prescribes no time limit for the President to act in this manner, and it applies to Ordinary Bills.
25.tq: Separate pocket veto from suspensive veto by focusing on the absence of a constitutional time limit.
25.sec: ■ Veto types → Bills  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of the qualified veto in the Indian constitutional system?
o: It involves the possibility of overriding the veto through a specified stronger majority.
It can be overridden by a higher majority.
It is recognised as a veto available to the President of India.
It is conceptually different from an absolute veto.
25.x: Qualified veto is an overridable veto by a higher majority, but it is not available to the President of India. Therefore, its recognition as an Indian presidential power is incorrect.
25.tq: Identify the exception by separating a general constitutional concept from the power actually available in India.
25.sec: ■ Veto types → Bills  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. In the case of a Money Bill, the President may either give assent or withhold assent.
2. The President may return a Money Bill for reconsideration under the suspensive veto.
3. The President is constitutionally bound to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: The President may assent to or withhold assent to a Money Bill but cannot return it for reconsideration. Under the Twenty-Fourth Amendment, assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill is mandatory.
25.tq: Use the Bill-type distinction: Money Bills cannot be returned, whereas Constitutional Amendment Bills require assent.
25.sec: ■ Veto types → Bills  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: The constitutional requirement that the President must give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill is associated with the:
25.x: The Twenty-Fourth Constitutional Amendment made it obligatory for the President to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill duly passed by Parliament.
25.tq: Use the amendment-number trap by linking the specific constitutional change to the correct amendment.
25.sec: ■ Veto types → Bills  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

25.s: The Eleventh Constitutional Amendment of 1961 is associated with which of the following changes?
o: Removal of nominated members from the Vice-Presidential electoral college
Providing for election of the Vice-President by State Legislatures
Ending the joint-meeting method for the election of the Vice-President
Introduction of direct election to the office of Vice-President
25.x: The Eleventh Amendment ended the earlier joint-meeting method and provided for election of the Vice-President by the members of both Houses of Parliament.
25.tq: Test the amendment by identifying the precise institutional procedure it altered, not the broader office concerned.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

25.s: Jagdeep Dhankhar’s resignation as Vice-President in July 2025 and the subsequent election of C. P. Radhakrishnan are relevant primarily to which constitutional provisions?
25.x: Articles 65 and 68 deal respectively with the Vice-President acting as President and the filling of a vacancy in the office of Vice-President. The July 2025 resignation therefore invoked these provisions.
25.tq: Use the office-function pairing: identify the Articles dealing with acting arrangements and a Vice-Presidential vacancy.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

25.s: C. P. Radhakrishnan became Vice-President of India after the resignation of Jagdeep Dhankhar. This was described as the:
o: First mid-term vacancy in the office of Vice-President
Second mid-term vacancy in the office of Vice-President
Third mid-term vacancy in the office of Vice-President
Fourth mid-term vacancy in the office of Vice-President
25.x: The resignation of Jagdeep Dhankhar and the election of C. P. Radhakrishnan constituted the third mid-term vacancy in the office of Vice-President.
25.tq: Treat the ordinal number as a direct quantitative fact and reject nearby sequential distractors.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

25.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the tenure of the President of India:
1. The Constitution prescribes no limit on the number of terms that a person may serve as President.
2. India follows an informal convention limiting the President to two terms.
3. The two-term limit is expressly imposed by a constitutional amendment.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
25.x: The Constitution does not prescribe a term limit for the President, although an informal convention of two terms is discussed. No constitutional amendment expressly imposes such a limit.
25.tq: Distinguish a constitutional rule from an informal convention and reject the amendment trap.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

25.s: Which of the following correctly states the comparison concerning presidential term limits?
o: The United States permits only one presidential term, whereas South Korea permits two five-year terms.
The United States limits a President to two terms, whereas South Korea provides for a single five-year term.
Both the United States and South Korea prescribe two presidential terms.
Both the United States and South Korea prescribe a single five-year presidential term.
25.x: The Twenty-Second Amendment of the United States limits a President to two terms. South Korea follows a single five-year presidential term.
25.tq: Handle comparison questions by checking both parts of the pair rather than recognising only one correct country.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

25.s: N. Sanjiva Reddy is associated with which one of the following distinctions?
o: Being the first Vice-President of India
Being the first nominated President of India
Being the only President of India elected unopposed
Being the first President elected directly by the people
25.x: N. Sanjiva Reddy holds the distinction of being the only President of India elected unopposed. He was elected President in 1977.
25.tq: Use the unique-distinction clue and reject options that confuse presidential and vice-presidential election methods.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

25.s: President Droupadi Murmu promulgated the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026. What change did the Ordinance provide?
o: Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, excluding the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 37 to 40, excluding the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, including the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 31 to 33, excluding the CJI
25.x: The 2026 Ordinance increased the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, with the Chief Justice of India excluded from this count.
25.tq: Separate the numerical change from the counting exception relating to the Chief Justice of India.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

25.s: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 was gazetted on:
25.x: The Ordinance was gazetted on 16 May 2026. The other dates relate to reports or commentary rather than the gazette date.
25.tq: Distinguish the official notification date from later reporting and criticism dates.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

25.s: The President addresses both Houses of Parliament assembled together at the commencement of the Budget Session under:
25.x: Article 87 provides for the President’s special address to both Houses assembled together at the commencement of the first session after each general election and the first session of each year, including the Budget Session context.
25.tq: Use the Article-number distinction among provisions dealing with parliamentary sessions, participation and ordinances.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

25.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Election method of the President of India — United States
Impeachment procedure of the President of India — Ireland
Election method of the President of India — Ireland
Impeachment procedure of the President of India — South Korea
25.x: The method of election of the President of India was borrowed from Ireland, whereas the impeachment procedure was borrowed from the United States.
25.tq: Start with the sure borrowing pair and guard against swapping the sources of election and impeachment.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

25.s: Epuru Sudhakar is associated with which constitutional issue?
25.x: The 2006 Epuru Sudhakar case concerned judicial review of the exercise of the pardoning power. It is associated with the constitutional limits on clemency decisions.
25.tq: Link the case name with its distinctive constitutional power instead of the office or emergency provisions.
25.sec: ■ Universal angles

26.s:
Under Article 72 of the Constitution, the President may exercise the power of pardon in which of the following cases?
1. Sentences awarded by a court-martial
2. Offences against a law relating to a matter within the Union executive power
3. All cases involving a death sentence
4. Sentences imposed under State laws in every case
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: Article 72 covers court-martial sentences, offences against Union laws and all death sentences. It does not cover sentences under State laws in every case.
26.tq: Separate the three constitutional grounds from the overbroad State-law statement.
26.sec: Pardoning power - Article 72, forms and nature

26.s: Which one of the following best describes a pardon?
o: Temporary stay of execution of a sentence
Reduction in the period of sentence without altering its character
Substitution of a lighter form of punishment
Removal of both the sentence and the conviction
26.x: A pardon removes both the sentence and the conviction and frees the person from all punishment.
26.tq: Distinguish the complete relief of pardon from the partial relief provided by other forms.
26.sec: Pardoning power - Article 72, forms and nature

26.s: The substitution of a lighter form of punishment for a heavier punishment is known as:
26.x: Commutation substitutes a lighter form of punishment, such as changing death sentence to rigorous imprisonment.
26.tq: Test the exact meaning of closely related legal terms.
26.sec: Pardoning power - Article 72, forms and nature

26.s: With reference to the President's pardoning power, which of the following statements is correct?
o: It is exercised on ministerial advice and is confined to the matters covered by Article 72(1)(a) to (c) and Union executive matters.
It is exercised independently of ministerial advice.
Amnesty is expressly included among the forms specified in Article 72.
It extends to every matter falling exclusively within State executive authority.
26.x: The President exercises the power on ministerial advice. Its constitutional scope is confined to Article 72(1)(a) to (c) and Union executive matters; amnesty is outside Article 72.
26.tq: Watch for the wrong-authority and overextension traps in constitutional powers.
26.sec: Pardoning power - Article 72, forms and nature

26.s: Which case held that the President may examine the evidence afresh while exercising the pardoning power, but that the convict has no right to an oral hearing?
26.x: In Kehar Singh (1989), the Supreme Court held that the President may examine the evidence afresh, but there is no right to an oral hearing.
26.tq: Link the judicial holding to the correct case name and year.

26.s: In which of the following circumstances may the exercise of the pardoning power be subjected to judicial review according to the principle laid down in Epuru Sudhakar (2006)?
o: When the decision is mala fide, arbitrary or based on irrelevant or extraneous grounds
Whenever the court disagrees with the quantum of punishment
Never, because clemency is a purely political power
Only when the convict has not been given an oral hearing
26.x: Epuru Sudhakar held that clemency may be reviewed when it is mala fide, arbitrary or based on irrelevant or extraneous considerations.
26.tq: Identify the limited grounds of judicial review instead of assuming total immunity or full appellate review.

26.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Articles 72 and 161:
1. The President may pardon a death sentence, whereas the Governor cannot pardon a death sentence.
2. The Governor may suspend, remit or commute a death sentence.
3. The Governor possesses the power to pardon a court-martial sentence.
4. Article 72 primarily relates to Union laws, while Article 161 relates to State laws.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The Governor has no power to pardon a death sentence or a court-martial sentence; statement 3 is false.
26.tq: Compare the two constitutional powers by law covered, death sentence and court-martial competence.

26.s: Parliament can promulgate an Ordinance under Article 123 only when:
o: either House of Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied that immediate action is necessary
the Supreme Court authorises the President to do so
the Council of States alone recommends immediate legislation
both Houses of Parliament are dissolved
26.x: An Ordinance may be promulgated when either House is not in session and the President is satisfied, on ministerial advice, that immediate action is necessary.
26.tq: Combine both mandatory conditions instead of treating dissolution as the sole requirement.

26.s: Which of the following statements regarding an Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 is correct?
o: It remains valid even if it violates Fundamental Rights.
It cannot amend or repeal an existing Act.
It has the force of an Act of Parliament while it remains operative.
26.x: An Ordinance has the force of an Act and may be retrospective or amend or repeal an Act, subject to constitutional limitations. It becomes void if beyond Parliament's competence or inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
26.tq: Reject absolute limitations and identify the legal effect of an Ordinance.

26.s: An Ordinance promulgated under Article 123 ordinarily ceases to operate:
o: six months after promulgation in every case
only when the President expressly withdraws it
six weeks after the earlier date of reassembly of Parliament
six weeks after the later date of reassembly of Parliament
26.x: An Ordinance ceases six weeks after the later date on which the two Houses reassemble. It may end earlier if disapproved or withdrawn.
26.tq: Focus on the later reassembly date and distinguish the ordinary period from the maximum possible life.

26.s: Which one of the following is NOT a constitutionally permissible limitation on an Ordinance?
o: It may be issued even when both Houses are in session if the President considers it convenient.
It must not violate Fundamental Rights.
It must satisfy the constitutional requirement of immediate action.
It must not be beyond Parliament's legislative competence.
26.x: An Ordinance cannot be promulgated when Parliament is in session. The other options describe applicable constitutional requirements or limitations.
26.tq: Find the statement that reverses the basic precondition for ordinance-making.

26.s: The power to promulgate Ordinances under Articles 123 and 213 was made non-justiciable by the:
26.x: The 38th Amendment Act, 1975 made the satisfaction under Articles 123, 213 and 352 non-justiciable. The 44th Amendment later undid this change.
26.tq: Discriminate between the amendment that created and the amendment that reversed the legal position.

26.s: Which constitutional amendment undid the non-justiciability introduced by the 38th Amendment in respect of the satisfaction under Articles 123, 213 and 352?
26.x: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 reversed the non-justiciability introduced by the 38th Amendment.
26.tq: Use the amendment sequence to avoid confusing the original change with its reversal.

26.s: The Supreme Court described repeated re-promulgation of Ordinances without placing them before the legislature as a fraud on the Constitution in:
o: State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu
26.x: In D.C. Wadhwa (1987), repeated re-promulgation without placing Ordinances before the legislature was characterised as a fraud on the Constitution.
26.tq: Match the distinctive judicial phrase with the case that first articulated it.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about Krishna Kumar Singh (2017):
1. Re-promulgation of an Ordinance may constitute a fraud on the Constitution.
2. Laying the Ordinance before the legislature is mandatory.
3. The President's satisfaction is completely beyond judicial review.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Krishna Kumar Singh held that re-promulgation can be a fraud on the Constitution and that laying before the legislature is mandatory. It also recognised that the satisfaction is open to judicial review, making statement 3 false.
26.tq: Use the judicial-review statement as the discriminator among otherwise correct holdings.

26.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Absolute veto — Indian President has no such power
Suspensive veto — Indian President may return a non-money Bill, but must assent if it is repassed
Pocket veto — Bill must be decided within ten days
Qualified veto — Indian President may override Parliament by a two-thirds majority
26.x: A suspensive veto permits return of a non-money Bill; if Parliament repasses it, with or without amendment, the President must assent. The Constitution does not prescribe a time limit for the pocket veto, and qualified veto is not held by the Indian President.
26.tq: Separate the four veto types by their effect and by whether the Indian President possesses them.
26.sec: Veto types - which the Indian President holds (Article 111)

26.s: Under Article 111, the President may do which of the following in relation to a non-money Bill?
o: Return it repeatedly until Parliament withdraws it
Assent, withhold assent or return it for reconsideration
Refer it compulsorily to the Supreme Court
Only assent or withhold assent, but never return it
26.x: Article 111 permits the President to assent to, withhold assent to, or return a non-money Bill for reconsideration.
26.tq: Recall the three textual alternatives in Article 111 and apply the money-Bill exception separately.
26.sec: Veto types - which the Indian President holds (Article 111)

26.s:
The absolute veto of the President may ordinarily operate in respect of which of the following situations?
1. A private member's Bill
2. A Government Bill when the Council of Ministers has resigned before assent
3. A Constitutional Amendment Bill
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: Absolute veto may apply to a private member's Bill and to a Government Bill when the Cabinet resigns before assent. A Constitutional Amendment Bill must receive assent.
26.tq: Apply the veto type to the special categories of Bills rather than to ordinary Bills generally.
26.sec: Veto types - which the Indian President holds (Article 111)

26.s: A pocket veto means that the President:
o: withholds assent permanently through an express order
rejects only Money Bills without recording reasons
returns a Bill once and then must assent if it is repassed
neither assents to, rejects nor returns the Bill, keeping it pending indefinitely
26.x: A pocket veto consists of taking no action—neither assent, rejection nor return—thereby keeping the Bill pending indefinitely.
26.tq: Distinguish inaction from express rejection and from the suspensive return of a Bill.

26.s: The possibility of a pocket veto by the President arises principally because:
o: the President has a constitutional power to dissolve Parliament
the Supreme Court authorises indefinite withholding of assent
Article 111 prescribes no time limit for presidential action on a Bill
Money Bills are valid for only ten days
26.x: Article 111 does not prescribe a time limit for the President's action, unlike the ten-day rule referred to in the United States context.
26.tq: Identify the constitutional omission that creates the practical power.

26.s: The only instance of a pocket veto at the Union level is associated with which President and which Bill?
o: Dr. Rajendra Prasad — Indian Telegraph Bill
Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed — Indian Post Office Bill
A.P.J. Abdul Kalam — Prevention of Terrorism Bill
Zail Singh — Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill
26.x: President Zail Singh used the pocket veto in 1986 in relation to the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill.
26.tq: Combine the office-holder, year and Bill to defeat near-name distractors.

26.s: Which statement correctly reflects the present constitutional position concerning a Governor's alleged pocket veto?
o: The Governor has the same indefinite pocket veto as the President.
The Governor has no pocket veto; indefinite inaction under Article 200 is justiciable.
The Governor may keep a Bill pending indefinitely without judicial scrutiny.
The Governor can exercise a pocket veto only over Money Bills.
26.x: The Supreme Court held in 2025 that indefinite inaction by the Governor under Article 200 is justiciable; therefore, the Governor does not possess a presidential-style pocket veto.
26.tq: Discriminate between the President's textual time-gap and the Governor's reviewable inaction.

26.s: Which of the following correctly describes the President's power over a Money Bill passed by Parliament?
o: The President must reject it if it was introduced on prior recommendation.
The President may return it for reconsideration but cannot reject it.
The President has no role after passage by Parliament.
The President may ratify or reject it, but cannot return it for reconsideration.
26.x: In relation to a Money Bill, the President may assent or withhold assent but cannot return it for reconsideration. Such Bills are generally introduced with prior recommendation.
26.tq: Use the Money Bill exception to the general return power under Article 111.
26.sec: Veto over money and constitutional amendment bills

26.s: With reference to a Constitutional Amendment Bill passed by Parliament, which one of the following is correct?
o: The President may reject it by absolute veto.
The President may return it once for reconsideration.
The President must give assent under the 24th Amendment, 1971.
The President may refer it to the Governor for advice.
26.x: The 24th Amendment, 1971 made presidential assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill mandatory; the President cannot reject or return it.
26.tq: Remember the special constitutional-amendment exception to presidential veto powers.
26.sec: Veto over money and constitutional amendment bills

26.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Returning a Bill for reconsideration is a one-time power of the President.
2. Financial Bills of Category I and Category II may be returned for reconsideration.
3. The President may return a Constitutional Amendment Bill for reconsideration.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: The return power is one-time and may apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II. A Constitutional Amendment Bill cannot be returned because assent is mandatory.
26.tq: Spot the special exception for Constitutional Amendment Bills among otherwise returnable Bills.
26.sec: Veto over money and constitutional amendment bills

26.s: A Bill passed by a State Legislature and reserved by the Governor for the consideration of the President is governed primarily by:
26.x: Article 201 deals with Bills reserved by the Governor for the consideration of the President.
26.tq: Match the constitutional Article with the stage at which a State Bill reaches the President.
26.sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

26.s: Under Article 200, the Governor must reserve a Bill for the consideration of the President when the Bill:
o: is a Money Bill passed by the State Legislature
has been passed unanimously by the State Legislature
endangers the position of the High Court
relates to a matter in the State List
26.x: The Governor must reserve a Bill that endangers the position of the High Court. Reservation is otherwise one of the constitutional choices available under Article 200.
26.tq: Identify the mandatory reservation case rather than an optional or unrelated category.
26.sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

26.s:
After a State Bill is reserved for the President's consideration under Article 201, which of the following powers does the President possess?
1. Assent to the Bill
2. Withhold assent
3. Direct the Governor to return a non-money Bill to the State Legislature
4. Remain bound to assent if the State Legislature repasses the Bill
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: The President may assent, withhold assent or direct return of a non-money Bill. The President is not bound to assent even if the State Legislature repasses it, making statement 4 false.
26.tq: Separate the President's Article 201 choices from the binding-assent rule applicable to an ordinary non-money Bill under Article 111.
26.sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

26.s: The President's power under Article 201 over a State Bill reserved by the Governor is regarded as an absolute veto because:
o: the President is not bound to assent even when the State Legislature repasses the Bill
the President can dissolve the State Legislature
the Governor cannot communicate with the President
the President can amend the Bill without legislative approval
26.x: Unlike the ordinary suspensive veto over a non-money parliamentary Bill, the President is not bound to assent to a reserved State Bill even after repassage.
26.tq: Compare the consequence of repassage under Article 201 with the ordinary suspensive veto.
26.sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

26.s: Under Article 201, the State Legislature is required to reconsider a non-money Bill returned by the President within:
26.x: Article 201 provides that the State Legislature should reconsider a non-money Bill returned by the President within six months.
26.tq: Recall the specific reconsideration period attached to a reserved State Bill.
26.sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

26.s: Which sequence correctly reflects the major developments concerning reserved Bills in Tamil Nadu described in the recent constitutional litigation?
o: Presidential Reference opinion — Supreme Court deemed assent — withholding of assent to anti-NEET Bill
Withholding of assent to anti-NEET Bill — Supreme Court deemed assent to ten repassed Bills — Presidential Reference opinion
Supreme Court deemed assent — withholding of assent to anti-NEET Bill — Presidential Reference opinion
Withholding of assent to anti-NEET Bill — Presidential Reference opinion — Supreme Court deemed assent
26.x: The sequence was withholding of assent to Tamil Nadu's anti-NEET Bill, the April 2025 Supreme Court order deeming ten repassed Bills assented using Article 142, and the November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion rejecting deemed assent as impermissible.
26.tq: Arrange the litigation by its dated stages and distinguish the later clarifying opinion from the earlier order.
26.sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

26.s: What was the significant holding of the Supreme Court in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu, as described in the constitutional developments of April 2025?
o: It abolished the Governor's power to reserve Bills.
It held that the President must assent to every repassed State Bill.
It held that all gubernatorial inaction is non-justiciable.
Using Article 142, it deemed ten repassed Bills to have received assent and set timelines.
26.x: In April 2025, the Supreme Court used Article 142 to deem ten repassed Tamil Nadu Bills assented and set timelines.
26.tq: Identify the unusual remedial action and the constitutional provision used by the Court.
26.sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

26.s: According to the Presidential Reference opinion of November 2025 under Article 143, which of the following statements is correct?
o: Courts may always prescribe fixed timelines for constitutional authorities.
Courts cannot fix timelines or grant deemed assent, although prolonged unexplained inaction may receive limited judicial review.
The President has no role in Bills reserved under Article 201.
Deemed assent is constitutionally permissible whenever a Governor delays action.
26.x: The November 2025 opinion stated that courts cannot fix timelines and that deemed assent is impermissible. It recognised limited review of prolonged unexplained inaction.
26.tq: Distinguish the later Presidential Reference position from the superseded approach in the earlier litigation.
26.sec: Veto over state bills reserved by the Governor - Article 201

26.s: Which recent development revived the debate on the possible misuse of the ordinance-making power and executive overreach?
o: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026
The Inter-State Water Disputes Amendment Ordinance, 2026
26.x: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 revived the debate on ordinance misuse and executive overreach.
26.tq: Identify the precise recent development instead of being misled by similarly worded legislative titles.

26.s: What is the principal criticism of the frequent promulgation of ordinances?
o: They can be issued only during a financial emergency.
They require prior approval from the Supreme Court.
They transfer all legislative powers to the States.
26.x: Frequent ordinances are criticised because they bypass parliamentary deliberation.
26.tq: Link the institutional criticism to the constitutional function being bypassed.

26.s: With reference to the veto power of the President of the United States, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: It is a pocket veto that can be overridden by a simple majority of Congress.
It is a suspensive veto that automatically becomes ineffective after thirty days.
It is a qualified veto that can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Congress.
It is an absolute veto that cannot be overridden by Congress.
26.x: The US President has only a qualified veto, which can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Congress.
26.tq: Discriminate between absolute, qualified, suspensive and pocket vetoes by focusing on the override condition.

26.s: The State ordinance concerning organ-transplant committees in Andhra Pradesh was issued under which Article of the Constitution?
26.x: A Governor's ordinance-making power for a State is exercised under Article 213; the Andhra Pradesh ordinance concerned organ-transplant committees.
26.tq: Use the Union ordinance–State ordinance distinction to identify the correct constitutional Article.

26.s:
Consider the following statements regarding ordinance-making powers:
1. The Union ordinance-making power is associated with Article 123.
2. The ordinance-making power of a State is associated with Article 213.
3. Frequent promulgation of ordinances has been criticised for bypassing parliamentary deliberation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
26.x: Statements 1 and 2 correctly identify the Union and State ordinance provisions, respectively. Statement 3 correctly states the principal criticism of frequent ordinances; therefore, all three statements are correct.
26.tq: Combine the Article distinction with the institutional criticism and check whether all three statements follow the constitutional comparison.

27.s: The Vice-President of India is elected by means of which electoral system?
o: Simple majority voting by secret ballot
Proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and open ballot
Proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and secret ballot
27.x: Article 66 provides for proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and the election is conducted by secret ballot.
27.tq: Discriminate between the voting method, ballot method and majority system rather than recalling only one feature.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: Which one of the following is NOT a qualification for election as Vice-President of India?
o: Qualification for election as a member of the Lok Sabha
Qualification for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha
27.x: The Vice-President must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old and qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha. Qualification for election to the Lok Sabha is not the prescribed condition.
27.tq: Find the one swapped constitutional qualification among closely related House requirements.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the normal term of office of the Vice-President of India?
o: Four years from the date of election, without continuation thereafter
Six years from entering office, with continuation only after parliamentary approval
Five years from the date of nomination, with no possibility of re-election
Five years from entering office, with continuation until the successor enters office
27.x: The Vice-President holds office for five years from the date of entering office and continues beyond that period until the successor enters office. The Vice-President is eligible for re-election any number of times.
27.tq: Separate the fixed term, commencement point and holdover provision instead of treating them as one date rule.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: The oath or affirmation of office to the Vice-President of India is administered by the
27.x: Article 69 provides that the oath or affirmation of office to the Vice-President is administered by the President or a person appointed by the President for that purpose.
27.tq: Apply the ‘who administers the oath?’ distinction among constitutional authorities.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the removal of the Vice-President of India:
1. The resolution must originate in the Rajya Sabha.
2. The resolution requires an effective majority of the Rajya Sabha.
3. The Lok Sabha must agree to the resolution by a simple majority.
4. The Constitution specifies grounds on which the Vice-President may be removed.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Removal is initiated in the Rajya Sabha, requires a majority of all the then members of that House, and must be agreed to by the Lok Sabha by simple majority. The Constitution does not state grounds for this removal.
27.tq: Break the removal procedure into origin, majority, second-House approval and grounds.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: A resolution for the removal of the Vice-President of India can be moved only after giving a minimum notice of
27.x: A minimum notice of 14 days is required before moving the resolution for removal of the Vice-President in the Rajya Sabha.
27.tq: Use the exact notice period as the decisive numerical discriminator.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: If the Vice-President of India is acting as President, who presides over the sittings of the Rajya Sabha?
o: The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
27.x: While acting as President, the Vice-President ceases to perform the functions of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Deputy Chairman presides over the Rajya Sabha during that period.
27.tq: Follow the consequence of temporary assumption of the President’s office on the Vice-President’s ex-officio role.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: While acting as President of India, the Vice-President is entitled to draw the salary of the
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
27.x: When acting as President, the Vice-President ceases to function as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and draws the President’s salary rather than the Chairman’s salary.
27.tq: Apply the office actually being performed, not the office ordinarily held.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: As Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, the Vice-President ordinarily exercises
o: A casting vote in the event of an equality of votes
A vote only on Money Bills
27.x: The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote when the votes are equally divided.
27.tq: Distinguish an ordinary vote from a casting vote in a presiding-officer question.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: A vacancy in the office of the Vice-President of India is to be filled
o: Within six months of the vacancy in every case
As soon as possible, without a constitutionally prescribed six-month deadline
Within one year, after approval by the Supreme Court
Only at the next general election to the Lok Sabha
27.x: Article 68 requires an election to fill a vacancy in the office of Vice-President as soon as possible. Unlike the vacancy in the office of President, no six-month deadline is prescribed for this election.
27.tq: Compare the vacancy rules for President and Vice-President, especially the presence or absence of a fixed deadline.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: When the office of the President falls vacant, the Vice-President acts as President until
o: The Council of Ministers elects a successor
The next session of Parliament begins
A new President is elected, which must take place within six months of the vacancy
The remaining term of the previous President expires
27.x: The Vice-President acts as President until a new President is elected. The election to fill the presidential vacancy must be held within six months of the vacancy.
27.tq: Identify the event that ends the acting arrangement and distinguish it from the former President’s remaining term.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: Which constitutional provision deals with disputes relating to the election of the Vice-President of India?
27.x: Article 71 places disputes relating to the election of the President or Vice-President under the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
27.tq: Match the constitutional function with its exact Article number rather than a neighbouring election Article.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding judicial authority over Presidential and Vice-Presidential election disputes:
1. The 39th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1975 removed the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction over such election disputes.
2. The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 restored that jurisdiction.
3. The Election Commission of India conducts these elections under the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: The 39th Amendment removed the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction over the specified election disputes, while the 44th Amendment restored it. The elections are conducted by the Election Commission under the 1952 Act.
27.tq: Arrange the amendment reversal and the conducting authority as separate legal facts.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: The Vice-President of India is ex officio President of which of the following bodies?
27.x: The Vice-President is also the ex-officio President of the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA).
27.tq: Use the exact institutional title to distinguish ICWA from other national bodies.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: According to Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, the total number of Union Ministers including the Prime Minister shall not exceed
o: 15 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
12 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
10 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
20 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
27.x: The 91st Amendment inserted Article 75(1A), limiting the Union Council of Ministers including the Prime Minister to 15 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
27.tq: Match the amendment with its exact percentage limit and constitutional Article.
27.sec: Size of the Council of Ministers - 91st Amendment and ranks  [APPSC]

27.s: If the total strength of the Lok Sabha is 543, the maximum permissible strength of the Union Council of Ministers including the Prime Minister is
27.x: Fifteen per cent of 543 is 81.45; the applicable maximum whole-number limit is 81 ministers, including the Prime Minister.
27.tq: Calculate the constitutional percentage cap and apply the whole-number limit.
27.sec: Size of the Council of Ministers - 91st Amendment and ranks  [APPSC]

27.s: A member of Parliament disqualified for defection under the Tenth Schedule is, by virtue of Article 75(1B),
o: eligible only after approval by the Election Commission
permanently barred from becoming a Union Minister
ineligible to be appointed Union Minister until re-elected to Parliament
eligible to be appointed Union Minister immediately after disqualification
27.x: Article 75(1B), inserted by the 91st Amendment, prevents a member disqualified for defection from being appointed a minister until re-elected to Parliament.
27.tq: Test the duration and condition of disqualification instead of treating it as a permanent bar.
27.sec: Size of the Council of Ministers - 91st Amendment and ranks  [APPSC]

27.s: With reference to the size of a State Council of Ministers, which one of the following is correct?
o: It shall not exceed 10 per cent of the Assembly strength and has no minimum floor.
It shall be fixed uniformly at 15 ministers for every State.
It shall not exceed 20 per cent of the Assembly strength, subject to a minimum of 10 ministers.
It shall not exceed 15 per cent of the Assembly strength, subject to a minimum of 12 ministers.
27.x: Article 164(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment, limits a State Council of Ministers to 15 per cent of the Assembly strength, while prescribing a minimum of 12 ministers.
27.tq: Check both limbs of the rule: the percentage ceiling and the statutory minimum floor.
27.sec: Size of the Council of Ministers - 91st Amendment and ranks  [APPSC]

27.s: The maximum number of ministers, including the Chief Minister, in a State having a Legislative Assembly strength of 294 is
27.x: Fifteen per cent of 294 is 44.1, giving a maximum of 44 ministers under the stated limit. The minimum floor of 12 does not affect this calculation.
27.tq: Apply the percentage cap to a State Assembly strength and distinguish it from the minimum floor.
27.sec: Size of the Council of Ministers - 91st Amendment and ranks  [APPSC]

27.s: Which one of the following is NOT a constitutionally prescribed rank of a Union Minister?
o: Minister of State with Independent Charge
27.x: The commonly recognised ranks are Cabinet Minister, Minister of State with Independent Charge, Minister of State and Deputy Minister. Deputy Prime Minister is not a constitutionally prescribed ministerial rank.
27.tq: Find the non-standard rank among the established ministerial categories.
27.sec: Size of the Council of Ministers - 91st Amendment and ranks  [APPSC]

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the classification of Union Ministers:
1. The Constitution itself classifies ministers into Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers.
2. The classification into ranks is based on convention and the choice of the Prime Minister.
3. Deputy Ministers form one of the conventionally recognised ministerial ranks.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: The Constitution does not itself classify ministers into ranks. The classification is based on convention and the Prime Minister’s choice, and Deputy Minister is one of the recognised ranks.
27.tq: Separate what the Constitution expressly provides from what operates through convention.
27.sec: Size of the Council of Ministers - 91st Amendment and ranks  [APPSC]

27.s: A full-strength Parliament consisting of 543 members in the Lok Sabha and 245 members in the Rajya Sabha would have how many members in the electoral college for the Vice-Presidential election?
27.x: The Vice-Presidential electoral college includes all members of both Houses, elected and nominated. Thus, 543 plus 245 gives a total of 788 members.
27.tq: Add both Houses and remember that nominated Parliamentary members are included.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Article 64 — Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
Article 67 — Oath or affirmation of the Vice-President
Article 71 — Election procedure by single transferable vote
27.x: Article 64 provides that the Vice-President shall be the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. Article 67 concerns term and removal, Article 69 concerns oath, and Article 71 concerns election disputes.
27.tq: Match each constitutional Article with its exact subject and reject neighbouring Article swaps.
27.sec: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes  [APPSC]

27.s: Under Article 75(5) of the Constitution of India, a person appointed as a Minister who is not a member of either House of Parliament must become a member within
27.x: Article 75(5) requires a non-member Minister to become a member of either House of Parliament within six consecutive months; otherwise, the person ceases to be a Minister.
27.tq: Use the precise constitutional time limit and distinguish it from other parliamentary periods.
27.sec: Article 75(5) - non-member minister

27.s: Which one of the following correctly states the ruling in S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001)?
o: A non-member cannot be repeatedly reappointed as Minister without getting elected.
Only a member of the Lok Sabha can be appointed as a Minister.
A non-member may be reappointed as Minister indefinitely without election.
A non-member cannot be appointed as Prime Minister under any circumstances.
27.x: The Supreme Court held that the constitutional provision for a non-member Minister cannot be used for repeated reappointments without the person securing election to the legislature.
27.tq: Discriminate the judicial limitation from the general six-month rule.
27.sec: Article 75(5) - non-member minister

27.s:
Consider the following statements regarding appointment of Ministers:
1. Any person may be appointed as a Minister, subject to the constitutional six-month rule.
2. A non-member Minister must become a member of either House of Parliament within six months.
3. The six-month rule does not apply to a person appointed as Prime Minister.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
27.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is false because the six-month rule applies to the Prime Minister as well.
27.tq: Find the exception that improperly excludes the Prime Minister from a general constitutional rule.
27.sec: Article 75(5) - non-member minister

27.s: The constitutional basis of the collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers is
27.x: Article 75(3) provides that the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People.
27.tq: Match the constitutional principle with the exact Article number.
27.sec: Council of Ministers - collective and individual responsibility

27.s: Which one of the following best represents individual responsibility of a Union Minister?
o: The Lok Sabha Speaker may dismiss a Minister for absence.
The Prime Minister may advise the removal of an individual Minister.
The entire Council must resign after defeat in a Rajya Sabha election.
The President may remove any Minister independently of the Prime Minister.
27.x: Individual ministerial responsibility is reflected in the Prime Minister's ability to have an individual Minister removed. The President formally removes the Minister on the Prime Minister's advice.
27.tq: Ask who would perform the personnel function in practice rather than relying only on formal wording.
27.sec: Council of Ministers - collective and individual responsibility

27.s: What is the constitutional consequence of the death or resignation of the Prime Minister?
o: The Rajya Sabha is automatically dissolved.
Only the Cabinet Secretariat is dissolved.
The Council of Ministers as a whole goes out of office.
The President assumes the office of Prime Minister permanently.
27.x: The Prime Minister is the head of the Council of Ministers; therefore, the death or resignation of the Prime Minister results in the Council of Ministers going out of office.
27.tq: Test the institutional consequence of the Prime Minister's departure.
27.sec: Council of Ministers - collective and individual responsibility

27.s: The oaths of office and secrecy to Union Ministers are administered by the
27.x: The President administers the oaths of office and secrecy to Union Ministers in accordance with the Third Schedule.
27.tq: Identify the constitutional authority associated with administering the oath.
27.sec: Council of Ministers - collective and individual responsibility

27.s: Under Article 74(1), the advice of the Council of Ministers becomes binding on the President after the President
o: secures approval from the Election Commission
refers the matter to the Supreme Court
obtains the consent of the Rajya Sabha
27.x: The President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice once, but must act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.
27.tq: Focus on the one permitted reconsideration rather than an unlimited presidential discretion.
27.sec: Articles 74, 77, 78 - content

27.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Article)
 a. Article 74(2)
 b. Article 77(1)
 c. Article 77(2)
 d. Article 77(3)

Communicating to the President decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to administration and legislative proposals
Administering the oath of office and secrecy to all Union Ministers

27.sec: Articles 74, 77, 78 - content

27.s:
Consider the following statements:

27.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the tenure of the Prime Minister?
o: The Prime Minister can be removed only by the Supreme Court.
The Prime Minister holds office for life unless removed by impeachment.
The Prime Minister continues in office while commanding the confidence of the Lok Sabha, subject to the President's pleasure in the constitutional sense.
The Prime Minister has a fixed tenure of five years irrespective of legislative support.
27.x: The Prime Minister has no fixed tenure and ordinarily continues while enjoying the confidence of the Lok Sabha. The Constitution formally states that Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure.
27.tq: Reject the fixed-term trap and connect tenure with legislative confidence.

27.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the President and the Prime Minister in the Indian parliamentary system?
o: The President is the de facto head of government and the Prime Minister is the de jure head of State.
The President is the de jure head of State and the Prime Minister is the de facto head of government.
The Prime Minister is the de jure head of State and the President is only a ceremonial officer of Parliament.
Both the President and the Prime Minister are de facto heads of government.
27.x: The President is the de jure head of the State, while the Prime Minister functions as the de facto head of government.

27.sec: Prime Minister - appointment, qualifications, oath, real executive

27.s: During a National Emergency, the President of India
o: acquires unrestricted discretion to disregard the advice of the Council of Ministers
continues to be bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers
becomes the real executive in place of the Prime Minister
may dismiss the entire Council without following constitutional advice
27.x: A National Emergency does not confer discretionary power on the President to disregard the binding advice of the Council of Ministers. The parliamentary executive relationship continues.
27.tq: Guard against the emergency-powers trap by checking whether the constitutional advice requirement has been altered.

o: collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha
the President's pleasure regarding the tenure of Ministers
the Prime Minister's duty to furnish information
27.x: Article 75(2) provides that Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, which operates in practice on the advice of the Prime Minister.

27.s: Who was the first Prime Minister of India and also holds the record for the longest overall tenure as Prime Minister?

Prime Minister with the shortest regular tenure
first acting Prime Minister of India, serving twice
first Prime Minister from the Rajya Sabha

27.tq: Distinguish a temporary office-holder from regular Prime Ministers using the specific numerical clue.

There is no constitutional term limit for the Prime Minister.

The President is both head of the State and head of government

Secretaries are not members of the legislature

All ministers are required to defend Cabinet decisions or resign

28.s: With reference to individual responsibility of a Union Minister, which of the following statements is correct?
o: A minister holds office during the pleasure of the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3).
A minister holds office during the pleasure of the President under Article 75(2).
A minister holds office during the pleasure of the Chief Justice of India.
A minister can be removed only after a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha.
